39331.e: SRG is the German abbreviation for the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation. SSR is the French abbreviation for Société suisse de radiodiffusion et télévision.
39331.m: The SRG is the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation.

39332.q: What did the SRG start with when it was founded in 1931?
39332.e: The SRG was formed in 1931 from regional radio companies. Television only came later.

39333.q: In which city is the SRG SSR based?
39333.e: The head office of the SRG SSR is in Bern. The studios of the individual language regions are in different cities.
39333.m: The SRG SSR is based in Bern.

39334.q: Which unit of the SRG makes radio and television in Romansh?
39334.e: RTR stands for Radiotelevisiun Svizra Rumantscha and broadcasts for Romansh-speaking Switzerland. SRF, RTS and RSI are responsible for German, French and Italian-speaking Switzerland.
39334.m: RTR is the SRG’s Romansh service.

39335.q: For which language region does RSI produce its programmes?
39335.e: RSI stands for Radiotelevisione svizzera di lingua italiana. It broadcasts from Ticino for Italian-speaking Switzerland.
39335.m: RSI is the radio and television of Italian-speaking Switzerland.

39336.q: For how many language regions does the SRG make its own programmes?
39336.e: SRF broadcasts for German-speaking Switzerland, RTS for French-speaking Switzerland, RSI for Italian-speaking Switzerland and RTR for Romansh-speaking Switzerland.
39336.m: The SRG broadcasts in all four national languages.

39337.q: Who is the SRG’s service SWI swissinfo.ch mainly intended for?
39337.e: SWI swissinfo.ch informs people abroad, especially Swiss citizens living abroad, about Switzerland. It is available in ten languages.
39337.m: Swissinfo informs the world about Switzerland in ten languages.

39338.q: What does the federal licence require of the SRG?
a: Programmes for all parts of the country and language regions
39338.e: The SRG has a public service remit. It is to provide all parts of the country and language regions with information, culture, education and entertainment.
39338.m: The SRG fulfils a public service remit for the whole of Switzerland.

39339.q: What legal form does the SRG SSR have?
39339.e: The SRG SSR is an association under the Civil Code. So it is not a federal office and not a profit-making company.
39339.m: The SRG SSR is organised as an association.

39340.q: Since 2019, which company collects the radio and television fee from households?
39340.e: Since 1 January 2019, Serafe AG has sent the bills to private households. For companies, the tax administration collects the fee.
39340.m: Serafe sends out the bills for the radio and television fee.

39341.q: Which company collected the radio and television licence fees until the end of 2018?
39341.e: Billag AG, a subsidiary of Swisscom, collected the fees from 1998. From 2019 another company took over this task.

39342.q: How many francs does a private household pay per year for the radio and television fee (as of 2026)?
39342.e: Since 2021, the fee for a private household has been 335 francs a year. That is just under 28 francs a month.
39342.m: A household pays 335 francs a year in radio and television fees.

39343.q: Since 2019, what decides whether a private household has to pay the fee?
a: Only the fact that the household exists
39343.e: In the past, only people who had registered a radio or television paid. Today basically every household pays, even without devices, because programmes can also be received on mobile phones and computers.
39343.m: The fee is paid per household, not per device.

39344.q: What was the result of the 2018 popular vote on the No Billag initiative?
a: Clearly rejected with about 72 per cent voting no
Narrowly rejected with 51 per cent voting no
Clearly accepted with 70 per cent voting yes
39344.e: The initiative wanted to abolish the licence fees. On 4 March 2018, about 72 per cent of voters rejected it.
39344.m: The No Billag initiative was clearly rejected in 2018.

39345.q: Who can be exempted from the radio and television fee?
a: Certain people with very little money
Everyone who has no mobile phone
39345.e: People who receive, for example, supplementary benefits to the AHV or disability insurance have very little money and can apply for exemption.
39345.m: People with very little money can be exempted from the fee.

39346.q: Do companies also have to pay a radio and television fee?
39346.e: Besides households, companies with a larger turnover also pay a fee. Small companies are exempt.
39346.m: Larger companies also pay a radio and television fee.

39347.q: Roughly what share of the income from the radio and television fee goes to the SRG?
39347.e: The SRG receives about 90 per cent of the income. Part of it goes to private local radio and regional television stations, which also have a public service remit.
39347.m: Private local radio and regional television also receive money from the fee.

39348.q: In 2019, the radio and television fee cost one franc a day. How much was that for the whole year?
39348.e: A year has 365 days. At one franc a day, that made 365 francs. From 2021 the fee was lowered to 335 francs.
39348.m: At first, the household fee cost one franc a day.

39349.e: Keystone-SDA collects news, pictures and videos and sells them to the media. It is the only full news agency in Switzerland.
39349.m: Keystone-SDA is Switzerland’s national news agency.

39350.q: What does the abbreviation SDA stand for?
39350.e: SDA stands for Schweizerische Depeschenagentur, the Swiss Dispatch Agency. A dispatch is an old word for a message sent quickly, for example by telegram.

39351.q: Why do newspapers buy reports from a news agency such as Keystone-SDA?
a: They do not have their own reporters everywhere
They are not allowed to write anything themselves
They get free paper that way
39351.e: No newspaper can have its own people everywhere. The agency reports from all over the country and sells its reports to many media outlets.
39351.m: News agencies supply reports where the media have no reporters of their own.

39352.q: What kind of company did the SDA merge with in 2018?
39352.e: In 2018, the SDA took over the picture agency Keystone. Since then the company has been called Keystone-SDA and supplies texts and photos.
39352.m: Keystone was a picture agency before it joined the SDA.

39353.q: In which city is Keystone-SDA based?
39353.e: Keystone-SDA is based in Bern. Since 2019 the newsroom has worked in the Wankdorf district.
39353.m: The news agency Keystone-SDA is based in Bern.

39354.q: In which languages does Keystone-SDA publish its reports?
39354.e: The agency reports in German, French and Italian. The French and Italian service is called Keystone-ATS.
39354.m: Keystone-SDA supplies news in three national languages.

39355.q: Who are a news agency’s most important customers?
a: Newspapers, radio stations and news websites
39355.e: Media outlets buy an agency’s reports and use them in full or in part. That way they can report on events where they have nobody of their own on the spot.
39355.m: News agencies supply other media with reports.

39356.q: Where does Keystone-SDA get many of its reports from distant countries?
39356.e: News agencies work together worldwide and exchange reports. That way Keystone-SDA can also report on events far away.

39357.q: What does the abbreviation “(sda)” at the end of a newspaper article mean?
a: The text comes from the news agency
The text is a letter to the editor
The text has not yet been checked
39357.e: With the abbreviation, a newspaper shows that it has taken the report from the agency. That way readers know where the information comes from.
39357.m: Agency abbreviations show where a report comes from.

a: False news that looks like real news
39358.e: Fake news is made-up or distorted reports that look like real news. It is often spread on purpose to deceive people.
39358.m: Fake news is false reports that are meant to look real.

a: A video or picture faked using artificial intelligence
A programme about the deep sea
39359.e: In a deepfake, artificial intelligence is used to change a face or voice so that it looks real. It can then look as if someone said something they never said.
39359.m: Deepfakes are convincing fakes made with artificial intelligence.

39360.q: On a website, what shows who is responsible for the content?
39360.e: The legal notice gives the name and address of the people responsible. If it is missing, that is a warning sign that the site might not be trustworthy.
39360.m: A look at the legal notice shows who is behind a website.

39361.q: What are texts called that deliberately try to make people laugh with made-up and exaggerated reports?
39361.e: Satire deliberately exaggerates in order to make fun of things that are wrong. It becomes a problem when someone takes it for real news and spreads it.
39361.m: Satire is deliberately exaggerated and not meant as real news.

39362.q: Why do false reports often spread especially fast on social media?
a: Because they trigger strong feelings such as anger or fear
Because they are always very short
Because they are only posted at night
Because they are shared by the authorities
39362.e: Reports that outrage or frighten people are shared more often. That way they reach very many people in a short time.
39362.m: We share what upsets us faster, even when it is false.

39363.q: A real photo from 2015 is now being shared as a picture from yesterday. What is the deception?
39363.e: The photo itself is real, but it is put in a false context. This is another way false reports arise.
39363.m: Even real pictures can deceive in a false context.

39364.q: What should you do before forwarding a surprising piece of news in the class chat?
a: Check whether reliable media are also reporting it
Send it to everyone straight away
Only look at the number of likes
39364.e: If well-known media are not reporting it, be careful. Checking first and sharing afterwards helps to stop false reports.

39365.q: What is a made-up warning called that is often forwarded like a chain letter?
39365.e: A hoax is a false report that spreads like a chain letter, for example a supposed virus warning. Often you are asked to forward it to as many people as possible.
39365.m: You should check a message first and only then share it.

39366.q: What does a fact check do?
a: It checks whether a claim is true
39366.e: In a fact check, a statement is compared with reliable sources. At the end there is a rating, for example “true”, “false” or “misleading”.
39366.m: A fact check tests claims against sources.

39367.q: Which tool helps you find out where a photo has appeared on the internet before?
39367.e: In a reverse image search, you upload a picture and search for identical pictures. That way you can see when and where it was first published.
39367.m: Reverse image search shows where a photo comes from.

a: The original source of a piece of information
The front page of a newspaper
39368.e: A primary source is, for example, an original study, the text of a law or an official statistic. If you read it, you are not relying only on how others report it.
39368.m: When checking, it helps to read the original source.

39369.q: In journalism, what does the two-source principle mean?
a: A piece of information needs two independent confirmations
You may only read two newspapers
39369.e: A piece of news should only be published once two independent sources confirm it. That lowers the risk of mistakes.
39369.m: Two independent sources make a report more reliable.

39370.q: Which body is best for checking a claim about the population of Switzerland?
a: A fan forum on the internet
39370.e: The Federal Statistical Office (FSO) collects and publishes official figures on the population. That makes it a reliable source.
39370.m: For official figures, the Federal Statistical Office is the right place to go.

39371.q: Which question is especially important when checking a report?
a: How many likes does it have?
39371.e: If you know who wrote a report, you can better judge whether the person or organisation is trustworthy and what their intentions are. Likes say nothing about the truth.
39371.m: When checking, always ask first who the sender is.

39372.q: What does it mean when a fact check rates a statement as “misleading”?
a: It is partly true but gives a false impression
39372.e: Misleading statements often contain real facts but leave out important things or present them in a distorted way. This creates a false picture.
39372.m: Even true figures can be presented in a misleading way.

39373.q: Why is a statistic without a source a problem for a fact check?
a: You cannot check where the figures come from
It is too easy to read
39373.e: Without a source, you do not know who collected the figures and how. So you cannot judge whether they are correct.
39373.m: Treat figures without a source with caution.

39374.q: What do many newspapers do before votes, because they receive especially many letters to the editor then?
a: They set a deadline before voting day
They stop printing letters to the editor altogether
They only print letters from the yes side
They charge a fee per letter
39374.e: Many newsrooms stop publishing new letters on the subject a few days before the vote. That leaves time to respond to claims.
39374.m: Before votes, there is often a deadline for letters to the editor.

39375.q: What may a newsroom usually do with a letter to the editor?
a: Shorten it without changing its meaning
Turn its opinion into the opposite
Put a different name under it
Write its own arguments into it
39375.e: Letters to the editor may be shortened if they are too long. But the meaning must be kept.
39375.m: A letter to the editor may be shortened, but not falsified.

39376.q: What is it called when an organisation has many similar letters to the editor sent in by different people?
39376.e: In a letter-writing campaign, many letters are meant to give the impression that an opinion is widespread. That is why newsrooms watch out for strikingly similar texts.
39376.m: Many identical letters to the editor can be part of an organised campaign.

39377.q: Under which section do letters to the editor appear in many newspapers?
39377.e: Many newspapers collect letters to the editor on a separate page, often called “Forum” or “Letters”. There, readers discuss things with each other.
39377.m: Letters to the editor are often on the newspaper’s forum page.

39378.q: What type of text is a letter to the editor?
39378.e: A letter to the editor expresses a personal opinion. Like a commentary, it is therefore one of the opinion-based types of text.
39378.m: A letter to the editor is an opinion-based text.

39379.q: What is the difference between a letter to the editor and a commentary in the newspaper?
a: A commentary is written by someone from the newsroom
A letter to the editor is always longer
A letter to the editor only appears online
39379.e: Both types of text contain opinions. But a commentary comes from a journalist, a letter to the editor from a member of the public.
39379.m: Commentaries are written by the newsroom, letters to the editor by the public.

39380.q: Why does a newspaper not print letters to the editor containing insults?
a: It shares responsibility for what it publishes
Letters to the editor may not contain opinions
The post does not deliver such letters
39380.e: Anyone who publishes an insult can share the blame, even if it came from someone else. That is why the newsroom checks letters to the editor before printing them.
39380.m: The newsroom is responsible for everything it prints.

39381.q: On news websites, what is the counterpart of the letter to the editor?
a: The reader comment under the article
39381.e: Online, readers can write their opinion directly under an article. These comments are also often checked by the newsroom.
39381.m: Online, readers write their opinion in the comments.

39382.q: What is the Swiss Press Council?
a: A complaints body for questions of media ethics
39382.e: The Press Council is a self-regulatory body of the media industry. It examines complaints about whether media have broken the rules of journalism.
39382.m: The Press Council watches over journalists’ professional ethics.

39383.q: What does the Swiss Press Council judge, for example?
a: Whether an article reports fairly and truthfully
Which sport is shown on television
39383.e: The Press Council examines complaints against the media. It judges whether a report keeps to the rules of journalism, for example the duty to tell the truth.
39383.m: The Press Council checks whether the media report fairly and truthfully.

39384.q: What are the rules that journalists should follow called?
39384.e: The journalists’ code describes the duties and rights of people working in the media. This includes, for example, the duty to tell the truth.
39384.m: The journalists’ code sets out the duties and rights of media workers.

39385.q: Which punishments can the Swiss Press Council impose?
39385.e: The Press Council cannot impose sanctions. But its statements have an effect, because the media concerned often publish them.
39385.m: The Press Council judges, but it does not punish.

39386.q: Who may file a complaint with the Swiss Press Council?
39386.e: Anyone can complain to the Press Council, even if they are not personally affected. That way the whole public can criticise the media.
39386.m: Anyone can complain to the Press Council.

39387.q: Who sits on the Swiss Press Council?
a: Media professionals and representatives of the public
39387.e: The Press Council has 21 members. Most of them work in the media themselves; some represent the public.
39387.m: Representatives of the public also sit on the Press Council.

39388.q: According to the journalists’ code, what must the media do if they have published a false report?
39388.e: The code requires materially false reports to be corrected. That way readers find out what is really true.
39388.m: Good media correct their mistakes publicly.

39389.q: Who supports the Swiss Press Council?
39389.e: Behind the Press Council is a foundation supported by journalists’ associations, publishers, editors-in-chief and the SRG. The state is not involved.
39389.m: The Press Council is an institution of the media industry itself.

39390.q: What does the principle of transparency in the federal administration mean?
a: Everyone may, in principle, see official documents
All Federal Council meetings are shown on television
All civil servants must work in public
Everyone may take part in votes in parliament
39390.e: Under the principle of transparency, everyone has access to official documents. They stay secret only in exceptional cases set out in law.
39390.m: Official documents are, in principle, open to everyone.

39391.q: Do you have to give a reason why you want to see an official document?
39391.e: Anyone who asks to see documents does not have to prove a special interest. Instead, the administration has to give reasons if it refuses access.
39391.m: No reason is needed to see official documents.

39392.q: Thanks to the principle of transparency, who may request documents from the federal administration?
39392.e: The Freedom of Information Act gives everyone the right of access. You do not have to be Swiss or have a particular job.

39393.q: Someone wants to know what a federal office has spent money on. What can this person do?
a: Ask the office to see the documents
Nothing at all, that stays secret
39393.e: Thanks to the principle of transparency, you can submit a request for access. The office must, in principle, show the documents.
39393.m: With a request, you can see official documents.

39394.q: Which principle applied in the federal administration before the principle of transparency?
a: The principle of separation of powers
39394.e: In the past, administrative documents were secret as a rule, unless they were specifically released. The Freedom of Information Act turned this the other way round.
39394.m: In the past, secrecy was the rule and openness the exception.

39395.q: What can you do if the federal administration refuses to let you see a document?
a: Ask for mediation and then go to court
Have the police search the office
39395.e: First there is a mediation procedure at an independent federal body. If that does not help, you can go to court.
39395.m: You can challenge a refusal to let you see documents.

39396.q: What does a request to see official federal documents usually cost today?
39396.e: After a change in the law that parliament decided in 2022, access is free of charge in principle. A fee can only be charged for especially time-consuming requests.
39396.m: Seeing federal documents is usually free.

39397.q: Why is the principle of transparency important for journalists?
a: They can request documents for their research
They receive money from the state
39397.e: With the principle of transparency, the media can check the work of the administration more closely. In this way they sometimes uncover mistakes or wrongdoing.
39397.m: The principle of transparency helps the media to keep a check on the administration.

39398.q: What is meant by “microtargeting” in an election campaign?
a: Advertising tailored specifically to small groups
A campaign only in small municipalities
A vote with only a few votes
39398.e: In microtargeting, data about interests and behaviour are used to send suitable messages to particular groups. So different people see different adverts.
39398.m: Microtargeting aims political advertising at small groups.

a: Automated accounts that post like humans
39399.e: Social bots are computer programs that automatically write, share or like posts on social networks. They can make an opinion seem more widespread than it is.
39399.m: Behind some accounts there is no person, but a program.

39400.q: What does the term “filter bubble” describe?
a: You mainly see content that matches your own opinion
A block for children on the internet
39400.e: Platforms often show posts that match what you already like. As a result, other points of view become visible less often.
39400.m: In a filter bubble you mainly see what is familiar and agrees with you.

39401.q: What is an “echo chamber” on social media?
a: A group of like-minded people who confirm each other’s views
39401.e: In an echo chamber, you mainly hear your own opinion echoed back by others. There is hardly any disagreement, and opinions can become stronger.
39401.m: In an echo chamber, only your own opinion echoes back.

39402.q: Why do political campaigns in Switzerland use social media and posters instead of TV adverts?
a: Political advertising on radio and television is banned
The Confederation pays for social media
39402.e: The Radio and Television Act bans political advertising on radio and television. That is why campaigns turn to posters, newspaper adverts and social media.
39402.m: In Switzerland there is no political advertising on radio and television.

39403.q: On many platforms, how can you recognise paid advertising posts?
a: By an especially large number of comments
By the time of the post
39403.e: Paid posts are marked with labels such as “Sponsored” or “Ad”. That way you know that someone has paid for them to be spread.

39404.q: What are people with many followers who can influence other people’s opinions called?
39404.e: Influencers reach many people through social media. That is why they are sometimes used in campaigns to promote causes.
39404.m: Influencers can shape opinions with their reach.

39405.q: What are hashtags such as #vote used for in political campaigns?
a: They make posts on a topic easy to find
They make posts free of charge
39405.e: A hashtag links a post to a topic. Anyone who searches for it finds all posts with this keyword.
39405.m: Hashtags gather posts on the same topic.

39406.q: Who often commissions opinion polls before votes?
39406.e: Media such as the SRG have polls carried out before votes. In this way they show the mood of the population.
39406.m: The media commission polls before votes.

39407.q: In a poll, what is a “sample”?
a: A selection of respondents meant to stand for everyone
39407.e: You cannot ask all voters. That is why a selection is asked that reflects the population as well as possible.
39407.m: A good sample reflects the whole population on a small scale.

39408.q: A poll shows 51 per cent yes with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. What does that mean?
a: The result is too close to say anything for sure
The proposal will definitely be accepted
The proposal will definitely be rejected
Exactly 51 per cent will vote yes
39408.e: The true yes share is probably between 48 and 54 per cent. Because 50 per cent lies within this range, the outcome is open.
39408.m: In close polls, the margin of error decides whether you can say anything.

39409.q: What can happen if people in a poll hide their true opinion because it is considered unpopular?
a: The poll automatically becomes more accurate
39409.e: Some people prefer to give the answer that goes down well socially. These are called socially desirable answers, and they can distort the result.
39409.m: Socially desirable answers can distort polls.

39410.q: Why can the result of a vote differ from the last poll?
a: Polls are snapshots and opinions change
The ballot papers are counted wrongly
39410.e: A poll only shows the mood at a particular point in time. Many people can still change their minds before voting day.
39410.m: A poll is a snapshot, not a forecast.

39411.q: Why is an online vote that anyone can take part in not representative?
a: There are too few possible answers
39411.e: In such votes, it is mainly people who are especially interested in the topic who take part. That is why they do not reflect the population properly.
39411.m: When people decide for themselves whether to take part, the result is distorted.

39412.q: Of 1,200 people asked, 660 say yes. What percentage is that?
39412.e: 660 divided by 1,200 makes 0.55. That is 55 per cent.
39412.m: To work out a percentage, divide the part by the whole and multiply by a hundred.

39413.q: With popular initiatives, what do experts often observe between the first poll and voting day?
39413.e: At first, many people like the idea behind an initiative. During the campaign, doubts often grow and the yes share falls.
39413.m: With initiatives, support often falls during the campaign.

39414.q: What are the weeks before a vote called, when people campaign with posters, adverts and events?
39414.e: In the referendum campaign, supporters and opponents try to convince voters of their view. Posters are an important tool for this.
39414.m: In the referendum campaign, both sides compete for votes.

39415.q: Why do large referendum campaigns now have to report who is paying for them?
a: So that voters can see who is behind a campaign
So that only rich people may advertise
So that the vote takes place earlier
39415.e: If you know who is paying for a campaign, you can judge its message better. The details are published by the Confederation.
39415.m: Large campaigns must disclose who is paying for them.

39416.q: A referendum poster shows an impressive figure without a source. What is the best way to deal with it?
a: Check the figure in reliable sources
Accept it as a fact straight away
Ignore it, because posters always lie
Look only at the colour of the poster
39416.e: Posters want to persuade and often only show part of the picture. If you check figures, for example in the Federal Council’s explanations or in the media, you can form your own opinion.
39416.m: Figures on posters are worth checking.

39417.q: What does a referendum poster that uses dark colours and threatening images want to achieve?
a: To stir up feelings such as fear or worry
To inform as neutrally as possible
39417.e: Posters often work with feelings instead of precise arguments. If you recognise this, you can look at the message more critically.
39417.m: Posters often appeal more to feelings than to reason.

39418.q: Why do referendum posters usually have short slogans and eye-catching pictures?
a: People only see them for a few seconds in passing
Posters may only have one word
39418.e: Posters are often only glanced at while walking or driving past. That is why the message must be understood immediately.
39418.m: A poster must get its message across in seconds.

39419.q: A campaign rents 400 poster sites at 250 francs each. How much does that cost in total?
39419.e: You calculate 400 times 250 francs. That makes 100,000 francs.
39419.m: Poster campaigns quickly cost a lot of money.

39420.q: After voting day, what else must larger referendum campaigns disclose?
39420.e: Before the vote, the planned budget is reported; afterwards, the final accounts. That way you can see how much money was actually used.
39420.m: After the vote, the final accounts show what a campaign cost.

39421.q: What does it mean when a party decides to leave the vote open (Stimmfreigabe)?
39421.e: When it leaves the vote open, a party does not give a voting recommendation. Each member then decides for themselves how to vote.
39421.m: When the vote is left open, each member decides for themselves.

39422.q: What can people demand if a media outlet has spread false facts about them?
a: A reply in the same media outlet
39422.e: Anyone directly affected by a presentation of facts in a media outlet can demand a right of reply. In it, their own view of the facts is published.
39422.m: The right of reply gives those affected a voice in the same media outlet.

39423.q: Which federal office supervises the radio and television broadcasters in Switzerland?
39423.e: The Federal Office of Communications (OFCOM) monitors, for example, whether broadcasters keep to their licences. It may not interfere with the content of the programmes.
39423.m: OFCOM supervises radio and television without dictating programmes.

39425.q: What are the media often called because they keep a check on government, parliament and the courts?
39425.e: Besides the legislature, the executive and the judiciary, independent media are seen as the fourth estate. They inform the public and uncover wrongdoing.
39425.m: The media are seen as the fourth estate.

39426.q: What is hidden advertising called that looks like a normal editorial article?
39426.e: Media should clearly separate advertising from editorial content. Hidden advertising deceives the audience and endangers independence.
39426.m: Advertising and journalism must be clearly separated.

39427.q: What does the Federal Constitution explicitly guarantee radio and television?
a: Independence and autonomy in making their programmes
A fixed number of advertising minutes
A seat in the Federal Council
39427.e: Article 93 of the Federal Constitution states that radio and television are independent and make their own programmes. The state may not dictate content to them.
39427.m: Radio and television make their programmes independently of the state.

39428.q: What is meant by media concentration?
a: A few companies own many media outlets
All media are based in one city
The media report on only one topic
39428.e: When a few publishers own many newspapers, the variety of voices shrinks. This can weaken the forming of opinions in a democracy.
39428.m: Media concentration reduces the variety of opinions.

39429.q: How do many newspapers earn their money?
a: With taxes set by the Federal Council
39429.e: Newspapers live mainly on readers who pay and on advertising. In 2022 the people rejected a media package with more state support.
39429.m: Newspapers are funded mainly by subscriptions and advertising.

39430.q: Today, how can a foreign woman who marries a Swiss man become Swiss?
a: Only if she lives in Bern
39430.e: Since 1992, marriage no longer automatically makes anyone Swiss. But spouses can be naturalised in a simplified way after a few years.
39430.m: Since 1992, marriage no longer automatically makes anyone Swiss.

39431.q: What is the municipality called whose citizenship a Swiss person holds?
39431.e: The place of origin (also place of citizenship) is written in the passport and identity card. It does not have to be where you live or were born.
39431.m: The place of origin is in the Swiss passport, even if you have never lived there.

39432.q: How does a child usually get Swiss citizenship if its mother is Swiss?
a: After living in Switzerland for ten years
39432.e: In Switzerland, citizenship is passed on by descent: a child of a Swiss mother is a Swiss citizen from birth. This also applies if the child is born abroad.
39432.m: Swiss parents pass on their citizenship to their children at birth.

39433.e: About 800,000 people with Swiss citizenship live abroad. They may also vote and stand for election from there.
39433.m: The Swiss abroad have a Swiss passport but live abroad.

39434.q: What is it called when a child gets its nationality from its parents?
39434.e: In Switzerland, the principle of descent applies: citizenship comes from the parents, not from the place of birth. In Latin it is called ius sanguinis.
39434.m: Under the principle of descent, you inherit citizenship from your parents.

39435.q: Which identity document do only Swiss citizens receive?
39435.e: Only people with Swiss citizenship get the Swiss passport and the Swiss identity card. Foreigners receive a foreign national’s permit.
39435.m: Only Swiss citizens receive a Swiss passport.

39436.q: Under what condition can you give up Swiss citizenship voluntarily?
a: If you have another nationality as well
If you have lost your passport
If you no longer want to vote
39436.e: You can only give up Swiss citizenship if you also hold another nationality. That way nobody becomes stateless.
39436.m: You can give up Swiss citizenship if you have another nationality.

39437.q: What is it called when a foreigner receives Swiss citizenship?
39437.e: Through naturalisation, a person without a Swiss passport receives citizenship. Afterwards they have the same political rights and duties as all Swiss citizens.
39437.m: Through naturalisation, you become a Swiss citizen.

39438.q: Which language skills do you need for naturalisation?
39438.e: Anyone who wants to be naturalised must be able to communicate in everyday life in a national language, that is German, French, Italian or Romansh.
39438.m: For naturalisation, you must speak a national language.

39439.q: Since 2018, which foreign national’s permit has been a requirement for ordinary naturalisation?
39439.e: Since 1 January 2018, only people with a C settlement permit can be naturalised. Before that, other permits were also enough.
39439.m: Without a C permit, there is no ordinary naturalisation.

39440.q: As a rule, how many years must you have lived in Switzerland to apply for ordinary naturalisation?
39440.e: Ordinary naturalisation requires 10 years of residence in Switzerland. Years between the 8th and 18th birthdays count double.
39440.m: Ordinary naturalisation requires 10 years of residence.

39441.q: A girl lives in Switzerland from her 8th to her 13th birthday, so 5 years. How many years are counted for her naturalisation?
39441.e: Years between 8 and 18 count double: 5 times 2 makes 10 years. However, the actual minimum stay of six years must still be met.
39441.m: Five years of childhood in Switzerland count as ten years.

39442.q: What did the Federal Supreme Court decide in 2003 in the case of the municipality of Emmen about naturalisations at the ballot box?
39442.e: In Emmen (LU), the people had rejected naturalisations at the ballot box without giving reasons. In 2003 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that a rejection must be justified and must not be arbitrary.
39442.m: A rejected naturalisation must be justified.

39443.q: Who decides on a simplified naturalisation, for example of spouses?
a: The federal State Secretariat for Migration
39443.e: In simplified naturalisation, the Confederation decides, more precisely the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). The canton is consulted beforehand.
39443.m: The Confederation decides on simplified naturalisation.

39444.q: How many years of marriage are needed for simplified naturalisation with a Swiss spouse who lives in Switzerland?
39444.e: Foreign spouses can apply for simplified naturalisation if they have been married for 3 years. In addition, they must have lived in Switzerland for a total of 5 years.
39444.m: Anyone married to a Swiss citizen can apply for simplified naturalisation.

39445.q: What usually happens to children under 18 when their parents are naturalised?
a: They are included in the naturalisation
They have to wait until they are 30
39445.e: Children under 18 who live with their parents are normally included in the parents’ application. They then become Swiss citizens together with them.
39445.m: Children are usually naturalised together with their parents.

39446.q: Which Federal Councillor gave up his Italian nationality before his election in 2017?
39446.e: Ignazio Cassis was a dual citizen of Switzerland and Italy. Before his election to the Federal Council in 2017, he voluntarily gave up his Italian passport, although the law does not require this.
39446.m: Dual citizens may also be elected to the Federal Council.

39447.e: A dual citizen holds the nationality of two countries, for example Switzerland and Italy. Switzerland allows this.

39448.q: What are Swiss citizens who live abroad called?
39448.e: About 800,000 Swiss citizens live abroad. They are called the Swiss abroad. Many of them are dual citizens.
39448.m: Swiss citizens living abroad are called the Swiss abroad.

39449.q: When you are naturalised in Switzerland, what decides whether you can keep your old nationality?
a: The law of your country of origin
Your mark in German at school
39449.e: Switzerland itself allows dual citizenship. But some countries take away their citizens’ nationality if they take on another one.
39449.m: Your country of origin decides whether you keep your old nationality.

39450.q: Does a dual citizen living in Switzerland basically have to do military service?
a: Yes, unless he has already served in the other country
Only if he lives in Bern
39450.e: Dual citizens living in Switzerland are also liable for military service. Anyone who has already done military service in the other country can be exempted.
39450.m: Dual citizens are also liable for military service in Switzerland.

39451.q: What is true of dual citizens in Switzerland?
a: They have all the rights of Swiss citizens
They may not have a Swiss passport
39451.e: Dual citizens are full Swiss citizens. They may vote and stand for election from the age of 18 and receive a Swiss passport.
39451.m: Dual citizens have the same rights in Switzerland as all Swiss citizens.

39452.q: From whom can Switzerland take away citizenship because of serious crimes such as terrorism?
a: Only from the Swiss abroad without a second passport
39452.e: Taking away citizenship is only possible for dual citizens, because nobody should become stateless. It is only considered for very serious crimes, for example terrorism.
39452.m: Swiss citizenship can only be taken away from dual citizens.

39453.q: In which booklet are the days of service completed by a member of the armed forces entered?
39453.e: The service record book shows, among other things, the days of service completed, the unit and the rank. It is important proof that the duty to serve has been fulfilled.
39453.m: The service record book records the days of service completed.

39454.q: What is the information event called that young Swiss men must attend before recruitment?
39454.e: On orientation day, young men find out how recruitment, military service, civilian service and civil protection work. It usually takes place in their canton of residence.
39454.m: Before recruitment, you attend the orientation day.

39455.q: What is the first basic military training in the Swiss Armed Forces called?
39455.e: Recruit school, RS for short, is the basic training for all new soldiers. There they learn the most important military skills.
39455.m: Every soldier begins with recruit school.

39456.q: What is the insurance called that replaces part of your wages during military service?
39456.e: The income compensation scheme (EO) pays members of the armed forces compensation for lost wages. People doing civilian service and civil protection also receive it.
39456.m: During service, the EO replaces part of your wages.

39457.q: What are the short periods of service that soldiers usually do every year after recruit school called?
39457.e: In the refresher course, WK for short, soldiers brush up their skills. For soldiers it usually lasts three weeks.
39457.m: Recruit school is followed by refresher courses.

39458.q: What are soldiers called who do all their military service in one go?
39458.e: Single-term servers complete all their days of service in one single block. After that they have completed their training service and go into the reserve.
39458.m: A Durchdiener does his military service in one go.

39459.q: What does the militia principle of the Swiss Armed Forces mean?
a: Most soldiers are citizens with a civilian job
The army consists only of volunteers
39459.e: In a militia army, citizens serve alongside their normal job. Only a small proportion of the members of the armed forces work for the army full-time.
39459.m: In the militia army, soldiers are ordinary working people in everyday life.

39460.q: After the army’s further development (WEA), roughly how many members should the Swiss Armed Forces have?
39460.e: With the further development of the army (WEA), the target strength was set at 100,000 members. In the past, the army was much bigger.
39460.m: The Swiss Armed Forces have a target strength of 100,000 members.

39461.q: What was the result of the popular vote of 22 September 2013 on abolishing compulsory military service?
39461.e: About three quarters of voters rejected the initiative. Compulsory military service for Swiss men therefore remained.
39461.m: Compulsory military service remained after a clear vote in 2013.

39462.q: What is the institution called, for example a hospital, where someone doing civilian service does their placement?
39462.e: People doing civilian service work in recognised host organisations, for example in care homes, hospitals or nature conservation organisations. The armoury and the barracks belong to the army.
39462.m: Civilian service is done in a recognised host organisation.

39463.q: Before civilian service was introduced, what happened to men who refused military service?
a: They were punished, often with prison
Nothing happened to them at all
39463.e: Before 1996, there was no civilian alternative service. Conscientious objectors were sentenced by military courts, often to prison.
39463.m: In the past, conscientious objectors in Switzerland went to prison.

39464.q: Can a soldier still switch to civilian service after recruit school?
a: Yes, an application is possible later too
Only if he is an officer
39464.e: You can apply to be admitted to civilian service after recruit school too. The days of military service already completed are counted.
39464.m: You can switch to civilian service even after recruit school.

39465.q: A soldier still has 100 days of military service to do and switches to civilian service. How many days of civilian service must he do?
39465.e: Civilian service lasts 1.5 times as long: 100 times 1.5 makes 150 days.
39465.m: Military service days times one and a half gives the civilian service days.

39466.q: Why does civilian service last longer than military service?
a: So that only those who are really serious switch
Because civilian servers work less per day
Because civilian servers have more holidays
39466.e: Anyone who accepts the longer civilian service shows that they cannot do military service for reasons of conscience. Since 2009 there has no longer been an examination before a commission.
39466.m: The longer period of service shows that you are serious about civilian service.

39467.q: Where, for example, do people do their civilian service?
39467.e: People doing civilian service work, for example, in old people’s homes, hospitals, schools or nature conservation. The barracks and the armoury belong to the army.
39467.m: Civilian servers help, for example, in care homes, hospitals or in nature.

39468.q: What do people doing civilian service learn in courses before their placement, for example?
a: How to look after people who need care
How to shoot an assault rifle
How to jump with a parachute
39468.e: Before their placements, civilian servers attend training courses, for example at Schwarzsee in the canton of Fribourg. There they learn, for instance, how to care for elderly or sick people.
39468.m: Civilian servers are prepared for their placements in courses.

39469.q: Which federal office is responsible for civilian service?
39469.e: The Federal Office for Civilian Service, ZIVI for short, organises the placements. It also examines applications for admission to civilian service.
39469.m: The Federal Office for Civilian Service organises civilian service placements.

39470.q: In Switzerland, who decides on changes to the Civilian Service Act?
a: The Federal Office for Civilian Service
39470.e: Federal laws are passed by the National Council and the Council of States. In 2020, for example, the National Council rejected a tightening of the Civilian Service Act.
39470.m: Federal laws are passed by parliament.

39471.q: What is the main task of civil protection?
a: To protect and care for the population in disasters
To put out fires in homes
39471.e: Civil protection helps in disasters and emergencies, for example floods. It looks after people and supports the fire brigade, the police and the health service.
39471.m: Civil protection protects and cares for the population in disasters.

39472.q: Who usually does civil protection service?
a: Men unfit for military service but fit for civil protection
All children from the age of 12
Only members of the fire brigade
39472.e: Anyone who, at recruitment, is found unfit for military service but fit for civil protection does civil protection service. Women and foreigners can volunteer.
39472.m: Those who do not have to join the army can serve in civil protection.

39473.q: What is the federal app called that gives information about dangers and alarms?
39473.e: The Alertswiss app of the Federal Office for Civil Protection sends out alarms, warnings and information. It adds to the sirens and the radio.
39473.m: Alertswiss informs you about alarms and dangers on your phone.

39474.q: Why are there especially many shelters in Switzerland?
a: So that almost all residents can find protection in an emergency
So that people can go on holiday there
So that cars can park there
So that banks can store money there
39474.e: Switzerland has about 9 million shelter places, more places than inhabitants (as of 2025). In principle, every resident should have a place near their home.
39474.m: Almost everyone in Switzerland has a place in a shelter.

39475.q: When does the siren test take place in Switzerland every year?
a: On the first Wednesday in February
On the first Monday in May
39475.e: On the first Wednesday in February, the sirens are tested throughout Switzerland. The test begins at 1.30 pm.
39475.m: The siren test is every year on the first Wednesday in February.

39476.q: What does the “general alarm” siren signal sound like?
a: A regular rising and falling wail
A hoot like a car horn
39476.e: In a general alarm, a rising and falling wail sounds for one minute. It means that there could be a danger to the population.
39476.m: A rising and falling wail means general alarm.

39477.q: What should you do if the general alarm sounds outside the siren test?
a: Listen to the radio and follow the instructions
39477.e: In a real alarm, you should listen to the radio or check the Alertswiss app and follow the authorities’ instructions. You should also tell your neighbours.
39477.m: In an alarm, you listen to the radio and follow the authorities’ instructions.

39478.q: Which siren signal warns of a flood wave near reservoirs?
39478.e: The water alarm consists of a series of low continuous tones. Anyone who hears it must leave the area at risk immediately.
39478.m: The water alarm warns of a flood wave from a reservoir.

39479.q: Who has to pay the military service exemption tax?
a: Swiss men who do neither military nor civilian service
Only soldiers on a refresher course
39479.e: The Federal Constitution says: Swiss men who do neither military nor alternative service owe a tax. This is the military service exemption tax.
39479.m: Anyone who does no service pays the military service exemption tax.

39480.q: What percentage of taxable income is the military service exemption tax (as of 2025)?
39480.e: The tax is 3 per cent of taxable income. It is based on the income for direct federal tax.
39480.m: The military service exemption tax is three per cent of taxable income.

39481.q: What is the minimum military service exemption tax per year in francs (as of 2025)?
39481.e: Even people who earn little pay a minimum of 400 francs a year. This minimum amount has existed since 2010.
39481.m: The military service exemption tax is at least 400 francs a year.

39482.q: A man does no service and has a taxable income of 50,000 francs. How much is his tax?
39482.e: 3 per cent of 50,000 francs is 50,000 times 0.03, so 1,500 francs. That is above the minimum amount.
39482.m: Three per cent of 50,000 francs is 1,500 francs.

39483.q: An apprentice liable for the tax has a taxable income of 10,000 francs. How much tax does he pay?
39483.e: 3 per cent of 10,000 francs would be 300 francs. Because the minimum amount is 400 francs, he pays 400 francs.
39483.m: With a small income, the minimum amount of the tax applies.

39484.q: Up to what age at most can you be liable for the exemption tax (as of 2025)?
39484.e: Liability for the tax lasts from age 19 to age 37 at the latest. In total, you pay no more than 11 annual amounts.
39484.m: Liability for the tax ends at 37 at the latest.

39485.q: What happens to the tax if someone liable for it does some of his days of service in a year?
a: It is transferred to the municipality
39485.e: Days of service completed reduce the tax. Depending on the number of days, it is reduced by one or more tenths.
39485.m: Anyone who does part of their service pays a smaller tax.

39486.q: Who is exempt from the military service exemption tax?
a: Anyone receiving a disability pension because of a significant disability
Anyone who likes to take long holidays often
Anyone who lives in a big city
39486.e: People with a significant disability who receive a disability pension do not have to pay anything. Anyone whose health was damaged during service is also exempt.
39486.m: People with a significant disability are exempt from the tax.

39487.q: Who has to pay church tax in Switzerland?
a: Members of a recognised national church
39487.e: In most cantons, church tax is paid by members of the recognised national churches. Anyone who leaves the church no longer has to pay it as a private individual.
39487.m: Church tax is paid by members of a recognised national church.

39488.q: Who pays tax on the wages of a 16-year-old apprentice?
a: The parents, together with their own wages
39488.e: The earned income of under-18s is taxed separately from their parents. That is why an apprentice, depending on the canton and the wage, fills in his own tax return.
39488.m: An apprentice pays tax on his wages himself.

39489.q: What is it called when the tax rate rises as income rises?
39489.e: With tax progression, you pay a higher percentage on higher incomes. That way people with a high income contribute more to the tasks of the state.
39489.m: Because of progression, the tax rate rises with income.

39490.q: Which key date usually decides in which canton you pay tax for a whole year?
39490.e: What counts is where you live at the end of the tax period, that is on 31 December. That is why anyone who moves in autumn pays tax for the whole year in the new canton.
39490.m: For tax, it is usually where you live on 31 December that counts.

39491.q: A toy costs 100 francs without VAT. How much does it cost with 8.1 per cent VAT?
39491.e: 8.1 per cent of 100 francs is 8.10 francs. 100 plus 8.10 makes 108.10 francs.
39491.m: On 100 francs, VAT comes to 8.10 francs.

39492.q: What does the tax office do if someone still does not submit a tax return after a reminder?
a: It estimates the taxes and can impose a fine
39492.e: Anyone who does not submit a tax return is assessed at the tax office's discretion. This means the tax office estimates their income and assets, and a fine may also be imposed.
39492.m: If you do not submit a tax return, the tax office assesses you.

39493.q: What is the tax called that is taken directly from the wages of foreign employees without a C permit?
39493.e: With tax at source, the employer takes the tax directly from the wages. It applies mainly to foreign employees without a settlement permit.
39493.m: With tax at source, the tax is taken directly from your wages.

39494.q: What is the 35 per cent tax called that is deducted, for example, from interest on savings accounts?
39494.e: Withholding tax is 35 per cent. Anyone who declares their savings correctly in their tax return gets it back.
39494.m: You get withholding tax back if you declare your assets honestly.

39495.q: Why do people pay different amounts of tax in different cantons?
a: Each canton sets its own tax rates
Because the federal government draws lots
Because taxes depend on the weather
Because each family decides for itself
39495.e: The cantons and municipalities have their own power to tax. That is why there are big differences between them, which is called tax competition.
39495.m: Each canton sets its own tax rates.

39496.q: Under HarmoS, how many years does primary school last, not counting kindergarten?
39496.e: Under HarmoS, the primary level including kindergarten lasts 8 years. 2 of those are kindergarten, which leaves 6 years of primary school.
39496.m: Under HarmoS, primary school lasts six years.

39497.q: Is going to a Gymnasium (academic upper secondary school) compulsory in Switzerland?
a: No, after compulsory school it is voluntary
39497.e: Compulsory schooling ends after lower secondary level. After that, young people choose, for example, an apprenticeship, a Gymnasium or a specialised upper secondary school.
39497.m: After compulsory school you can choose between an apprenticeship and further schools.

39498.q: What are the days off called that pupils in many cantons may take without giving a reason?
39498.e: In many cantons, schoolchildren may take a few joker days each school year. Parents have to tell the school beforehand.
39498.m: With a joker day you may take a school day off without giving a reason.

39499.q: How do the cantons work together on school matters?
39499.e: The cantons work together in the Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education (EDK). It drew up the HarmoS agreement, for example.
39499.m: The cantons work together on education in the EDK.

39500.q: What is the agreement between the cantons called that harmonises things like school starting age and the length of school levels?
39500.e: The HarmoS agreement is an agreement between cantons to harmonise compulsory schooling. It came into force in 2009.
39500.m: With HarmoS, many cantons brought their schools into line.

39501.q: Who does compulsory schooling apply to in Switzerland?
a: All children who live in Switzerland
39501.e: Compulsory schooling does not depend on nationality. All children who live here have the right and the duty to go to school.
39501.m: Compulsory schooling applies to all children in Switzerland.

39502.q: Under HarmoS, how many years does lower secondary level last?
39502.e: After primary level comes lower secondary level, which lasts three years under HarmoS. When it ends, compulsory schooling is over.
39502.m: Lower secondary level lasts three years.

39503.q: In some cantons, are parents allowed to teach their children at home?
a: Yes, with a permit and under supervision
Yes, without any rules at all
39503.e: Home schooling is allowed, restricted or almost banned, depending on the canton. Where it is allowed, a permit and checks by the authorities are usually needed.
39503.m: Each canton decides for itself whether home schooling is allowed.

39504.q: What was the result of the first federal vote on a voting age of 18 in 1979?
39504.e: In 1979 the people and the cantons narrowly rejected lowering the voting age. It was only accepted at the second attempt.
39504.m: The voting age of 18 took two attempts in Switzerland.

39505.q: What was the voting age at federal level before 1991?
39505.e: Until 1991 you could only vote in votes and elections from the age of 20. Then the voting age was lowered to 18.
39505.m: In the past you could only vote in Switzerland from the age of 20.

39506.q: What was lowered to 18 first in Switzerland?
a: The voting age at federal level
Both on exactly the same day
The age for a driving licence
39506.e: The voting age was lowered to 18 in 1991. The age of majority only followed in 1996.
39506.m: In Switzerland, voting from 18 came before adulthood from 18.

39507.q: What is voting over the internet called, which is being tested in some cantons?
39507.e: With e-voting you cast your vote electronically. Because security is very important, it is only being tested in a few cantons and under strict conditions.
39507.m: With e-voting you vote over the internet.

39508.q: Apart from being 18, what do you need to have the right to vote at federal level?
39508.e: According to the Federal Constitution, Swiss citizens aged 18 and over have the right to vote. Foreigners may not vote at federal level, even if they have lived here for a long time.
39508.m: At federal level, only Swiss citizens aged 18 and over may vote.

39509.q: What does the active right to vote mean?
a: You may pass laws on your own
39509.e: With the active right to vote you may cast your vote and, for example, elect members of the National Council. At federal level you get it at 18.
39509.m: With the active right to vote you may go and vote.

39510.q: What does the passive right to vote mean?
a: You may be elected to an office
You may only vote by post
39510.e: The passive right to vote is the right to stand for election. At federal level you get it at 18, like the right to vote.
39510.m: If you have the passive right to vote, you may stand for election.

39511.q: What was the result of the 1991 vote on a voting age of 18?
a: The people and the cantons clearly said yes
Only the people said yes, the cantons said no
39511.e: On 3 March 1991 about 73 per cent voted yes, and all the cantons agreed as well. Since then you may vote at federal level from 18.
39511.m: In 1991 a clear majority said yes to a voting age of 18.

39512.q: What does the right to vote on issues mean, compared with the right to elect?
a: You decide on issues such as laws
You elect people to an office
39512.e: With the right to vote on issues you take part in votes on matters such as initiatives or laws. With the right to elect you choose people, for example for the National Council.
39512.m: Votes are about issues, elections are about people.

39513.q: Why can the canton of Glarus have a lower voting age than the federal government?
a: The cantons set their own rules on political rights in cantonal matters
Because Glarus is not part of Switzerland
Because the Federal Council decides it again every year
Because there are no laws in Glarus
39513.e: The Federal Constitution leaves the rules for votes and elections in cantonal and municipal matters to the cantons. That is why the cantons can set their own voting age.
39513.m: Each canton decides from what age you may vote in cantonal matters.

39514.q: In the canton of Glarus, may 16-year-olds also vote at municipal assemblies?
a: Yes, it also applies to the municipalities
Only if their parents are there
No, only in the neighbouring canton
39514.e: In Glarus, the voting age of 16 applies to cantonal and municipal matters. So young people can also have a say in their municipality.
39514.m: In Glarus, 16-year-olds may also vote in their municipality.

39515.q: From what age could young people in Germany vote in the 2024 European elections?
39515.e: For the 2024 European elections, Germany lowered the voting age to 16. For elections to the Bundestag, however, it is still 18.
39515.m: In the 2024 European elections, 16-year-olds could already vote in Germany.

39516.q: In which referendum in Scotland in 2014 could 16-year-olds already vote?
a: In the referendum on the euro
In the election of the British king
In the referendum on joining the EU
39516.e: In the 2014 independence referendum, 16- and 17-year-olds in Scotland could vote for the first time. The majority voted against independence.
39516.m: In Scotland, 16-year-olds could vote on independence in 2014.

39517.q: In Brazil, young people aged 16 and over may vote “voluntarily”. What does that mean?
a: They may vote, but they do not have to
They must vote, otherwise they are fined
They may only vote with their parents
They may only vote at school
39517.e: Voluntary means you may, but you do not have to. In Brazil, 16- and 17-year-olds may vote, and from 18 voting is compulsory there.
39517.m: In Brazil, 16-year-olds may already vote voluntarily.

39518.q: Which of Switzerland's neighbouring countries lowered the voting age to 16 nationwide in the same year as Glarus?
39518.e: In 2007 Austria introduced a voting age of 16 for all national elections. This made it one of the first countries in Europe to do so.
39518.m: Austria has had a voting age of 16 across the whole country since 2007.

39519.q: What is an argument often given for a voting age of 16?
a: Young people should have a say earlier in questions that affect their future
Young people then have to pay taxes
Young people may then drive a car
Young people then no longer have to go to school
39519.e: Supporters say young people are affected by many decisions for a long time and should have a say. Opponents think the voting age and the age of majority should be the same.
39519.m: The voting age of 16 is about whether young people should have a say earlier.

39520.q: Why are provisionally admitted people allowed to stay in Switzerland?
a: Returning to their country would be too dangerous
39520.e: Provisionally admitted people would actually have to leave Switzerland. But because of war or great danger in their home country, that cannot reasonably be expected.
39520.m: Provisionally admitted people cannot go back because of danger.

39521.q: Which permit is the residence permit?
39521.e: The B permit is the residence permit for foreigners who live in Switzerland for a longer time, for example for a job.
39521.m: The B permit is a residence permit for a limited time.

39522.q: What is the most important difference between the B permit and the C permit?
a: B is for a limited time, C is unlimited
B is for children, C for adults
B is only valid in summer, C only in winter
B is for tourists, C for Swiss people
39522.e: The B residence permit has to be renewed regularly. The C settlement permit, on the other hand, has no time limit.
39522.m: The B permit has to be renewed, the C permit is unlimited.

39523.q: How long is the B permit valid for citizens of EU and EFTA states?
39523.e: The B residence permit for EU/EFTA citizens is valid for five years. It can be extended for another five years.
39523.m: The B permit for EU citizens is valid for five years.

39524.q: After how many years of residence do foreigners usually get the C permit at the earliest?
39524.e: Normally ten years of residence and good integration are needed. For citizens of some states and for especially good integration, it is possible after only five years.
39524.m: You usually get the C permit after ten years.

39526.q: Which permit do people get who work in Switzerland only for a short time, usually less than a year?
39526.e: The L permit is the short-term residence permit. It applies to limited stays of usually less than a year.
39526.m: The L permit is meant for a short stay.

39527.q: Which permit did many refugees from Ukraine receive from 2022?
39527.e: Protection status S was activated for the first time in March 2022. It gives people seeking protection from Ukraine a quick right to stay without the normal asylum procedure.
39527.m: Refugees from Ukraine received protection status S.

39528.q: Which authorities issue residence and settlement permits in Switzerland?
39528.e: The permits are issued by the cantons' migration offices. At federal level, the State Secretariat for Migration is responsible.
39528.m: The cantonal migration offices issue permits for foreigners.

39529.q: Which national colours did the Helvetic Republic choose?
39529.e: The Helvetic Republic chose green, red and yellow as its national colours. The white cross on a red background only became the symbol of all of Switzerland later.
39529.m: The colours of the Helvetic Republic were green, red and yellow.

39530.q: In which town was the Helvetic Republic founded on 12 April 1798?
39530.e: 121 delegates proclaimed the republic in Aarau. This made Aarau the first, provisional capital.
39530.m: Aarau was the first capital of the Helvetic Republic.

39531.q: What kind of state was the Helvetic Republic?
39531.e: The Helvetic Republic was run centrally by one government. The cantons were only administrative districts without any power of their own.
39531.m: In the Helvetic Republic the cantons had no power of their own.

39532.q: Which country had a great influence on the Helvetic Republic?
39532.e: In 1798 French troops occupied Switzerland. The Helvetic Republic was built on the model of France.
39532.m: The Helvetic Republic came about under the influence of France.

39533.q: Who ended the Helvetic Republic in 1803 and gave Switzerland a new order?
39533.e: In 1803 Napoleon put the Act of Mediation into force. This ended the Helvetic Republic, and the cantons got more power again.
39533.m: Napoleon ended the Helvetic Republic in 1803.

39534.q: What happened to the subject territories in the Helvetic Republic?
39534.e: The first Helvetic constitution removed the difference between ruling cantons and subjects. All citizens got equal rights.
39534.m: Since 1798 there have been no subject territories in Switzerland.

39535.q: Which part of the country fiercely resisted the French in September 1798 and was brutally crushed?
39535.e: Nidwalden rejected the Helvetic constitution and rose up. On 9 September 1798 French troops crushed the uprising with great violence.
39535.m: The days of terror in Nidwalden in 1798 cost many people their lives.

39536.q: Roughly how long did the Helvetic Republic last?
39536.e: The Helvetic Republic was founded in 1798 and ended in 1803. So it only lasted about five years.
39536.m: The Helvetic Republic lasted from 1798 to 1803.

39537.q: Who issued the Act of Mediation for Switzerland in 1803?
39537.e: Napoleon Bonaparte handed over the Act of Mediation on 19 February 1803. With it he ended the turmoil of the Helvetic Republic.
39537.m: In 1803 Napoleon gave Switzerland a new order with the Act of Mediation.

39538.q: How many cantons did Switzerland have after the Act of Mediation of 1803?
39538.e: The 13 old cantons were restored and six new cantons were created. Together that made 13 + 6 = 19 cantons.
39538.m: The Act of Mediation created a Switzerland with 19 cantons.

39539.q: Which of these cantons was newly created by the Act of Mediation in 1803?
39539.e: Aargau was created in 1803 as one of six new cantons. Valais, Geneva and Neuchâtel only joined the Confederation in 1815.
39539.m: Aargau has been a canton of its own since 1803.

39540.q: Which canton south of the Alps was created in 1803 from former subject territories?
39540.e: Ticino had previously been a subject territory of the Confederates. With the Act of Mediation it became a canton with equal rights in 1803.
39540.m: Ticino has been a canton of its own since 1803.

39541.q: What is the period from 1803 to 1813 called in Swiss history?
39541.e: The Mediation period begins with Napoleon's Act of Mediation of 1803. It ends after his defeat in 1813.
39541.m: The Mediation period lasted from 1803 to 1813.

39542.q: What was the assembly of cantonal envoys called during the Mediation period?
39542.e: Envoys from the cantons met in the Diet. They voted according to the instructions of their cantonal governments.
39542.m: The Diet was the assembly of the cantonal envoys.

39543.q: What replaced the order of the Act of Mediation after Napoleon's fall?
39543.e: After Napoleon's defeat in 1813, the Act of Mediation lost its support. The Federal Treaty of 1815 made Switzerland a loose alliance again.
39543.m: The Mediation period was followed by the Federal Treaty of 1815.

39544.q: How many cantons belonged to the Sonderbund?
39544.e: The Sonderbund was made up of Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais. Obwalden and Nidwalden were counted together as Unterwalden.
39544.m: Seven Catholic cantons formed the Sonderbund.

39545.q: Which cantons joined together in the Sonderbund?
39545.e: The Catholic conservative cantons feared a strong federal state under liberal leadership. That is why they founded the Sonderbund in 1845.
39545.m: The Sonderbund was an alliance of Catholic conservative cantons.

39546.q: Who led the federal troops as general in the Sonderbund War?
39546.e: General Dufour fought the war quickly and tried to avoid casualties. The Dufourspitze is also named after him.
39546.m: General Dufour won the Sonderbund War.

39548.q: How did the Sonderbund War end?
a: With victory for the federal troops
39548.e: The federal troops under General Dufour won quickly, among other places at the battle of Gisikon near Lucerne.
39548.m: The federal troops won the Sonderbund War.

39549.q: What was created in 1848, shortly after the Sonderbund War?
39549.e: After the war, Switzerland gave itself a Federal Constitution in 1848. The loose confederation of states became a federal state.
39549.m: After the Sonderbund War, the federal state was created in 1848.

39555.q: Who elected the first seven Federal Councillors in November 1848?
39555.e: On 16 November 1848 the National Council and the Council of States together elected the first seven Federal Councillors. The Federal Council is still elected this way today.
39555.m: Already in 1848, parliament elected the Federal Council.

39556.q: What became the same throughout Switzerland from 1850, after the federal state was founded?
39556.e: Before that, the cantons had their own coins. The Coinage Act of 1850 made the franc the common currency.
39556.m: Since 1850 people have paid with francs all over Switzerland.

39558.q: Under the 1848 constitution, who was allowed to vote in elections and on issues at federal level?
39558.e: The 1848 constitution gave the right to vote and elect only to Swiss men. Women remained excluded for a long time.
39558.m: In 1848 only men had political rights at federal level.

39559.q: Since what year has Bern been the seat of the Federal Council and parliament?
39559.e: Shortly after the federal state was founded, the Federal Assembly chose Bern as the seat of the federal authorities in November 1848.
39559.m: Bern has been the federal city since 1848.

39560.q: Which city received the second most votes in the National Council when the federal city was chosen in 1848?
39560.e: In the National Council, Bern received 58 votes, Zurich 35 and Lucerne 6. This made Zurich the strongest rival.
39560.m: Zurich lost to Bern in the choice of federal city in 1848.

39561.q: Why is Bern officially called the “federal city” and not the “capital”?
a: Out of consideration for the cantons
Because Bern is not a canton
Because a court wanted it that way
39561.e: According to the federalist idea, no city should stand above the others. That is why people speak of the federal city as the seat of the federal authorities.
39561.m: Bern is the federal city so that no canton stands above the others.

39562.q: Which university did Zurich receive, in a way, as compensation for Bern becoming the federal city?
39562.e: In 1855 the federal government founded the Federal Polytechnic School in Zurich, today's ETH. It was the first federal university.
39562.m: ETH Zurich is the oldest federal university.

39564.q: Why did Lucerne have hardly any chance of becoming the federal city in 1848?
39564.e: Lucerne had been the leading canton of the defeated Sonderbund. Shortly after the war, the majority did not want to make this city the seat of the federal state.
39564.m: As a former Sonderbund city, Lucerne had no chance in 1848.

39565.q: Which argument spoke especially in favour of Bern as the federal city in 1848?
a: Bern links German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland
39565.e: Bern lies on the border between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland. After the civil war, this was meant to strengthen the unity of the country.
39565.m: Bern is seen as a bridge between German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandy.

39566.q: What does today's Federal Constitution say about a capital of Switzerland?
39566.e: None of the three Federal Constitutions has named a capital or federal city. Bern is the federal city because of the decision of 1848.
39566.m: The Federal Constitution does not name a capital of Switzerland.

39567.q: What is the complete revision of the Federal Constitution in 1874, which brought the optional referendum, called?
39567.e: In 1874 the whole Federal Constitution was rewritten, which means it was totally revised. The optional referendum on laws was added at that time.
39567.m: With the total revision of 1874, the people got more rights.

39568.q: What can the people have a say on with the treaty referendum?
a: The election of the Federal Council
Rulings of the Federal Supreme Court
39568.e: With the treaty referendum, the people can vote on important treaties with other states. This right has existed since 1921.
39568.m: The people can also have a say on important international treaties.

39569.q: Which movement campaigned in the 1860s for more people's rights such as the referendum?
39569.e: The Democratic Movement first campaigned for direct people's rights in cantons such as Zurich. Its ideas went into the Federal Constitution of 1874.
39569.m: The Democratic Movement demanded more say for the people.

39570.q: How many signatures does an optional referendum need today (as of 2026)?
39570.e: Since 1977, 50,000 valid signatures have been needed. Before that, fewer were enough.

39572.q: How many cantons are needed to call a cantonal referendum at federal level?
39572.e: Instead of 50,000 signatures, 8 cantons can also demand the referendum together. But this happens very rarely.

39573.q: What happens to a new federal law if no referendum is called within the deadline?
a: It comes into force without a vote
It goes to the people anyway
39573.e: The referendum is voluntary, which means optional. If nobody collects enough signatures, the law can apply without a popular vote.
39573.m: Without a referendum, a law does not need a popular vote.

39574.q: Which court became a permanent court with the Federal Constitution of 1874?
39574.e: Before 1874, the Federal Supreme Court only met when needed. With the new constitution it got permanent judges and a permanent seat.
39574.m: Since 1874 the Federal Supreme Court has been a permanent court.

39575.q: What can you demand with the popular initiative introduced in 1891?
a: A change to the Federal Constitution
The removal of the Federal Council
39575.e: Since 1891 the people have been able to propose changing individual articles of the Federal Constitution or adding new ones. This is called a partial revision.
39575.m: With a popular initiative you can change the Federal Constitution.

39576.q: Does the Federal Council have to agree to a popular initiative before the people can vote on it?
a: No, enough valid signatures are sufficient
Yes, and the Federal Supreme Court too
39576.e: If an initiative gets 100,000 valid signatures, a vote is held. The Federal Council and parliament may give a recommendation, but they cannot prevent the vote.
39576.m: With enough signatures, an initiative goes to the people.

39577.q: What does a total revision of the Federal Constitution mean?
39577.e: In a total revision, the whole Federal Constitution is renewed. If only part of it is changed, it is called a partial revision.
39577.m: In a total revision, the whole constitution is renewed.

39579.q: What happens if the people and the cantons accept a popular initiative?
a: Its text goes into the Federal Constitution
The Federal Council has to resign
There are new elections straight away
Nothing, it is only a wish
39579.e: If an initiative is accepted, its text becomes part of the Federal Constitution. Parliament and the Federal Council then have to put it into practice.
39579.m: An accepted initiative changes the Federal Constitution.

39580.q: What can you not demand directly with a popular initiative at federal level?
39580.e: An initiative for a law only exists in the cantons. Several attempts to introduce it at federal level as well have failed.
39580.m: At federal level there is no initiative for a law.

39581.q: What can parliament put forward against a popular initiative?
39581.e: Parliament can draw up its own proposal on the same topic. Then the people vote on both proposals.
39581.m: A counter-proposal is parliament's proposal on the same question.

39582.q: What does it mean when a committee “launches” a popular initiative?
39582.e: Launching means starting. The initiative is published in the Federal Gazette, and from then on signatures may be collected for 18 months.
39582.m: The launch is when collecting signatures begins.

39583.q: In which year did the national general strike take place in Switzerland?
39583.e: In November 1918, just after the end of the First World War, many workers stopped work.
39583.m: The national general strike was in 1918.

39584.q: What did people do during the national general strike?
39584.e: In a strike, people deliberately do not work in order to push through their demands. In 1918 a great many workers went on strike all over Switzerland.
39584.m: In a strike, people stop work.

39585.q: Whom did the Federal Council send against the strikers in 1918?
39585.e: The Federal Council called up the army to end the strike. After three days the strikers called off the strike.
39585.m: The Federal Council used the army against the national general strike.

39586.q: Which demand of the national general strike was fulfilled later?
39586.e: The strikers demanded, among other things, women's right to vote, the AHV and a 48-hour week. Much of this only came years later.
39586.m: Many demands of the national general strike were put into practice later.

39587.q: What working week did the strikers demand in 1918?
39587.e: At that time people often worked much longer. The 48-hour week was largely introduced in 1919 and 1920.
39587.m: The national general strike demanded a 48-hour week.

39588.q: Which disease raged in 1918 and killed about 22,000 people in Switzerland?
39588.e: The flu pandemic also hit the soldiers who had been called up. About 1,500 soldiers died of it.
