39588.m: Spanish flu killed many people in Switzerland in 1918.

39589.q: Which war was just ending when the national general strike began?
39589.e: On 11 November 1918 the First World War ended with the armistice. After years of hardship, the mood among workers was very tense.
39589.m: The national general strike began one day after the end of the First World War.

39590.q: How are seats distributed in a proportional election?
a: According to the lists' share of the votes
39590.e: Each list receives roughly as many seats as matches its share of the votes. This means smaller parties are represented too.
39590.m: In a proportional election, the seats match the share of the votes.

39591.q: What is the voting system called that was used to elect the National Council before 1919?
39591.e: In majority voting, whoever has the most votes wins. This favoured the big parties, above all the Radicals.
39591.m: Before proportional voting, the National Council was elected by majority voting.

39592.q: Which chamber of the federal parliament is elected by proportional representation?
39592.e: The National Council is elected by proportional representation. The seats are distributed according to the lists' share of the votes. Most cantons elect the Council of States by majority voting.
39592.m: The National Council is elected by proportional representation.

39593.q: In a proportional election, what may you do when you “panache”?
a: Write names from other lists onto your list
Write one person twice on the list
Put in a blank ballot paper
Go to the ballot box twice
39593.e: When you panache, you add candidates from other party lists to your ballot paper. This lets you vote for people from different parties.
39593.m: Panaching means mixing names from different lists.

39594.q: What does cumulating mean in a proportional election?
a: Writing one person twice on the list
Crossing a person off the list
39594.e: When you cumulate, you write a person's name a second time on the ballot paper. That way they get two votes.
39594.m: Cumulating means giving one person two votes.

39595.q: A party gets 40 per cent of the votes in a proportional election. There are 10 seats. Roughly how many seats does it get?
39595.e: In a proportional election, the seats roughly match the share of the votes. 40 per cent of 10 seats is 4 seats.
39595.m: In a proportional election, the seats match the share of the votes.

39596.q: Which parties usually have an advantage in a majority election?
39596.e: In a majority election, whoever has the most votes wins. Small parties often end up with nothing. Proportional voting gives them a chance too.
39596.m: Proportional voting gives small parties a chance too.

39597.q: How many seats does the National Council have today?
39597.e: The National Council has 200 seats. They are distributed among the cantons according to population and elected by proportional representation.

39599.q: Which fundamental right in the Federal Constitution did the Federal Supreme Court find was violated in Appenzell Innerrhoden in 1990?
39599.e: The Federal Constitution requires women and men to have equal rights. Excluding women from the right to vote went against this.
39599.m: Women and men have equal political rights in Switzerland.

39600.q: Which court decided in 1990 that women in Appenzell Innerrhoden may vote?
39600.e: The Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne decided in favour of the women at the end of November 1990. This gave them political rights throughout the country.
39600.m: The Federal Supreme Court brought women's suffrage to Innerrhoden in 1990.

39601.q: Where did the men of Appenzell Innerrhoden reject women's right to vote in April 1990?
39601.e: In Innerrhoden, people vote at the Landsgemeinde in the open air. On 29 April 1990 the men said no there once again.
39601.m: At the Landsgemeinde, people vote by raising their hands.

39602.q: Who filed the complaint against Appenzell Innerrhoden at the Federal Supreme Court?
39602.e: Women from the canton fought their exclusion in court. They relied on equality in the Federal Constitution.
39602.m: Brave women from Innerrhoden won their right to vote in court.

39603.q: How many years after federal women's suffrage in 1971 did women in Appenzell Innerrhoden get the right to vote in the canton?
39603.e: The calculation is 1990 minus 1971 = 19. For that long, women in Innerrhoden could vote at federal level but not in their canton.
39603.m: Women in Innerrhoden waited 19 years longer for the cantonal right to vote.

39604.q: Which canton was the first to introduce women's right to vote, in 1959?
39604.e: Vaud introduced women's suffrage on 1 February 1959. Neuchâtel and Geneva soon followed.
39604.m: In 1959 Vaud was the first canton with women's suffrage.

39605.q: Which neighbouring canton introduced women's right to vote at its Landsgemeinde in 1989?
39605.e: The Landsgemeinde of Ausserrhoden narrowly agreed in April 1989. That left only Innerrhoden.
39605.m: Appenzell Ausserrhoden introduced women's suffrage in 1989.

39606.q: Since what date has Jura been a canton of its own?
39606.e: On 1 January 1979 the canton of Jura became sovereign. This makes it the youngest canton in Switzerland.
39606.m: The canton of Jura has existed since 1 January 1979.

39607.q: In which year did the Swiss people approve the founding of the canton of Jura?
39607.e: On 24 September 1978 the people and all the cantons agreed. The Federal Constitution had to be changed for this.
39607.m: All of Switzerland voted on the new canton in 1978.

39608.q: Who was allowed to vote on founding the canton of Jura in 1978?
39608.e: For a new canton, the Federal Constitution had to be changed. That is why all the Swiss people and all the cantons voted in 1978 and said yes.
39608.m: All of Switzerland voted on the new canton of Jura.

39609.q: Which congress gave the Jura region to the canton of Bern in 1815?
39609.e: After Napoleon's defeat, the great powers reorganised Europe. In the process, the Jura region went to Bern.
39609.m: The Congress of Vienna gave the Jura to Bern in 1815.

39611.q: Which canton did the canton of Jura separate from?
39611.e: The Jura had belonged to the canton of Bern since 1815. Many people in the Jura wanted a canton of their own, and in 1979 it was created.
39611.m: The canton of Jura used to belong to Bern.

39613.q: Which town moved from the canton of Bern to the canton of Jura on 1 January 2026?
39613.e: The voters of Moutier decided to change cantons. Since 1 January 2026 Moutier has belonged to the canton of Jura.
39613.m: Moutier has belonged to the canton of Jura since 2026.

39614.q: How many large buildings make up the Federal Palace in Bern?
39614.e: The Federal Palace is made up of the Federal Palace West, the Parliament Building in the middle and the Federal Palace East.
39614.m: The Federal Palace has three buildings: West, the Parliament Building and East.

39616.q: Who mainly works in the Federal Palace West and the Federal Palace East today?
a: The Federal Council and the federal administration
39616.e: Members of the Federal Council and parts of their departments have their offices in the two side wings. Parliament meets in the building in the middle.
39616.m: The Federal Council and the administration work in the Federal Palace West and East.

39617.q: What is the big square in front of the Federal Palace in Bern called?
39617.e: The Bundesplatz lies in front of the Parliament Building. Demonstrations, markets and festivals also take place there.
39617.m: The Bundesplatz lies in front of the Federal Palace.

39618.q: Which landscape does the large painting in the National Council chamber show?
39618.e: The large picture shows Lake Uri with the Rütli and the Mythen peaks. It is a reminder of the beginnings of the Swiss Confederation.
39618.m: A large picture of Lake Uri with the Rütli hangs in the National Council chamber.

39619.q: What does the mural in the Council of States chamber show?
39619.e: Albert Welti and Wilhelm Balmer painted a Landsgemeinde from the 18th century. After Welti's death, Balmer completed the work by 1914.
39619.m: In the Council of States chamber you can see a Landsgemeinde.

39620.q: Which statue stands in the domed hall of the Federal Palace?
39620.e: A group of figures showing three Confederates stands in the domed hall. It is a reminder of the alliance of the founding cantons.
39620.m: The three Confederates stand in the domed hall.

39621.q: Roughly how long is the whole row of buildings of the Federal Palace?
39621.e: The Federal Palace West, the Parliament Building and the Federal Palace East together form a front of a little more than 300 metres. It stands high above the Aare.
39621.m: Altogether the Federal Palace is over 300 metres long.

39623.q: For how many years is the President of the USA elected?
39623.e: The US President's term of office lasts four years. The election is held in early November.
39623.m: A US President is elected for four years.

39624.q: Who appoints the judges of the Supreme Court of the USA?
a: The President with the approval of the Senate
39624.e: The President proposes a person, and then the Senate has to agree. Supreme Court judges stay in office for life.
39624.m: US Supreme Court judges are appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

39625.q: What is the minimum number of electoral votes needed to become US President?
39625.e: The Electoral College has 538 members. Whoever gets an absolute majority, which means at least 270 votes, becomes President.
39625.m: A candidate needs at least 270 electoral votes to become President.

39626.q: With which procedure can Congress remove a US President for serious offences?
39626.e: In impeachment, the House of Representatives brings the charges and the Senate decides with a two-thirds majority.
39626.m: A US President can be removed through impeachment.

39627.q: On which day does a newly elected US President take office?
39627.e: Since 1937, 20 January after the election has been inauguration day. The President then takes the oath of office in Washington.
39627.m: A new US President is sworn in on 20 January.

39628.q: Who takes over if a US President dies during their term of office?
39628.e: The Vice President is first in line of succession. For example, Lyndon B. Johnson became President in 1963 after the death of John F. Kennedy.
39628.m: If the US President dies, the Vice President takes over.

39629.q: What is the minimum age to become President of the USA?
39629.e: The constitution requires a minimum age of 35. You also have to be a US citizen from birth and have lived in the USA for 14 years.
39629.m: A US President must be at least 35 years old.

39630.q: What is typical of a presidential system like the one in the USA?
a: Parliament cannot simply vote the government out.
The head of government is elected by parliament.
Parliament can be dissolved at any time.
39630.e: In a presidential system, the president is elected independently of parliament. He stays in office for the whole term, even if parliament has a different majority.
39630.m: In a presidential system, government and parliament are strongly separated.

39631.q: How many members does the US Senate have?
39631.e: The Senate has 100 senators. It is seen as the more respected of the two chambers.

39632.q: How many senators does each US state send to the Senate?
39632.e: Each state sends the same number of representatives, however big it is. This is similar to the Council of States in Switzerland, where most cantons have two seats.
39632.m: Each US state has two senators.

39633.q: What are the two chambers of the US Congress called?
a: National Council and Council of States
House of Commons and House of Lords
39633.e: The US Congress is made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives. Together they pass the laws.
39633.m: The US Congress is made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

39634.q: What is the main task of the US Congress?
39634.e: Congress is the parliament of the USA. It passes the laws, and the President leads the government.
39634.m: The US Congress passes the laws.

39635.q: Which Swiss chamber is the US Senate most similar to?
39635.e: In the US Senate, each state has two seats, however big it is. In the Council of States, most cantons also have two seats.
39635.m: The US Senate is similar to the Swiss Council of States.

39636.q: In which building in Washington does the US Congress meet?
39636.e: The building with its large dome stands on Capitol Hill. The Senate and the House of Representatives have their chambers there.
39636.m: The US Congress meets in the Capitol in Washington.

39637.q: Which chamber of the US Congress has fewer members?
a: Neither, there is only one chamber
39637.e: The Senate has 100 members, the House of Representatives 435 voting members. So the Senate is the smaller chamber.
39637.m: The US Senate is smaller than the House of Representatives.

39638.q: Who in the USA can stop a law passed by Congress with a veto?
39638.e: The President can reject a law with a veto. With a large majority, however, Congress can override the veto.
39638.m: The US President can use a veto.

39639.q: What is the building called in which the British Parliament meets?
39639.e: The British Parliament meets in the Palace of Westminster on the Thames in London. It includes the famous clock tower with the bell Big Ben.
39639.m: The British Parliament meets in the Palace of Westminster.

39640.q: What is the elected chamber of the British Parliament called?
39640.e: The House of Commons is the lower house. Its members are elected by the people, and it is the more powerful chamber.
39640.m: The elected British lower house is called the House of Commons.

39641.q: How are most members of the British upper house chosen?
a: They are elected by the people.
They are elected by the municipalities.
39641.e: Most members of the House of Lords are appointed for life. There are also some bishops of the Church of England.
39641.m: Members of the House of Lords are mostly appointed, not elected.

39642.q: How many seats does the British House of Commons have?
39642.e: The House of Commons has 650 seats. Each seat belongs to a constituency in the United Kingdom.
39642.m: The British House of Commons has 650 members.

39643.q: Which voting system is used to elect the members of the British House of Commons?
a: Election by the House of Lords
39643.e: In each constituency, whoever gets the most votes wins, even without an absolute majority. This is called “first past the post”.
39643.m: In each constituency for the House of Commons, the person with the most votes wins.

39644.q: What is special about the constitution of the United Kingdom?
a: It is not written down in a single document.
It is the longest constitution in the world.
39644.e: The British constitution is made up of many laws, court rulings and customs. There is no single constitutional document like the one in Switzerland.
39644.m: Britain has no constitution in a single document.

39645.q: What is the “shadow cabinet” in the British Parliament?
a: The opposition group that mirrors the ministerial posts
A secret committee of the intelligence service
The ministers of the regions Scotland and Wales
39645.e: The largest opposition party names a spokesperson for each ministry. That way a possible alternative government is ready.
39645.m: The shadow cabinet is the opposition's rival team to the government.

39646.q: Which part of the United Kingdom has had its own parliament in Edinburgh again since 1999?
39646.e: Since 1999 Scotland has had its own parliament with powers over things like schools and health. This handing over of power to the parts of the country is called devolution.
39646.m: Scotland has had its own parliament in Edinburgh since 1999.

39647.q: Which parliament is often called the “Mother of Parliaments”?
39647.e: The British Parliament has a very long history. Many countries, such as Canada, Australia and India, have modelled their parliaments on it.
39647.m: The British Parliament is known as the “Mother of Parliaments”.

a: A kingdom in which a constitution limits the monarch's power
A state without a king but with a constitution
A kingdom in which the king decides everything alone
A state in which the people elect the king every year
39648.e: In a constitutional monarchy, even the monarch has to keep to the constitution.
39648.m: In a constitutional monarchy, the monarch is bound by the constitution.

39649.q: Who is head of state of the United Kingdom (as of 2025)?
39649.e: Charles III became King in September 2022 after the death of his mother Elizabeth II. He is also head of state of other countries such as Canada and Australia.
39649.m: Since 2022 Charles III has been King of the United Kingdom.

39650.q: Which of Switzerland's neighbouring states is a monarchy?
39650.e: Liechtenstein is a principality with a prince as head of state. Its constitution combines the monarchy with democratic rights for the people.
39650.m: As a principality, Liechtenstein is a monarchy.

39651.q: Which of these countries is a constitutional monarchy?
39651.e: Spain has a king as head of state, but it is governed by an elected government. Germany, Italy and Portugal are republics.
39651.m: Spain is a kingdom with a constitution and a parliament.

39652.q: What is the main task of a monarch in a parliamentary monarchy?
a: Leading the army in war personally
Running the daily work of government
39652.e: The monarch receives guests, opens parliament and represents the country. The political decisions are made by the elected government.
39652.m: A monarch in a parliamentary monarchy mainly represents the state.

39653.q: What title does the head of state of Japan have?
39653.e: Japan is a constitutional monarchy with an emperor, the Tenno. According to the constitution, he only has symbolic tasks.
39653.m: Japan's head of state is an emperor.

39654.q: What is a monarchy called in which the ruler has unlimited power?
39654.e: In an absolute monarchy, the ruler is not bound by any constitution. A well-known example is Louis XIV of France.
39654.m: In an absolute monarchy, the ruler has all the power.

39655.q: Who makes the political decisions in Britain?
39655.e: Britain is a constitutional monarchy. The King represents the country, but the political decisions are made by the government.
39655.m: In Britain the elected government governs, not the King.

39656.q: What does the Latin expression “res publica”, from which the word republic comes, mean?
39656.e: “Res publica” translates as “the public matter”. So the state should be a matter for all citizens.
39656.m: Republic comes from the Latin “res publica”, the public matter.

39657.q: What makes a republic different from a monarchy?
a: The head of state is chosen for a limited time and does not inherit the office.
There are no laws in a republic.
There is no parliament in a republic.
A republic always has an emperor.
39657.e: In a monarchy, the head of state is usually determined by inheritance. In a republic, they are elected or appointed for a limited time.
39657.m: In a republic, nobody inherits the office of head of state.

39658.q: What form of state does Switzerland have?
39658.e: Switzerland is a federal republic. There is no hereditary head of state, but an elected Federal Council.

39659.q: Which Italian city was a powerful republic for over a thousand years until Napoleon ended it in 1797?
39659.e: The Republic of Venice was led by an elected Doge and was a great trading power. In 1797 Napoleon conquered the city.
39659.m: Venice was an independent republic until 1797.

39660.q: Which of Switzerland's neighbouring countries became a republic in 1918 after the end of the Habsburg monarchy?
39660.e: After the First World War, Austria-Hungary fell apart. On 12 November 1918 the Republic of German-Austria was proclaimed.
39660.m: Austria has been a republic since 1918.

39661.q: How did Italy decide on its form of state in 1946?
a: By an order from the King
By a decision of the army
39661.e: On 2 June 1946 a majority of Italians voted for the republic. The King had to leave the country.
39661.m: Italy became a republic in 1946 through a referendum.

39662.q: During which event did France become a republic for the first time?
39662.e: During the French Revolution the monarchy was abolished in 1792. King Louis XVI was executed in January 1793.
39662.m: France first became a republic in the French Revolution.

39663.q: Which republic existed on the territory of Switzerland from 1798 to 1803?
39663.e: After the French invasion, the old Confederation became the Helvetic Republic in 1798. It was a unitary state and ended in 1803 with the Act of Mediation.
39663.m: The Helvetic Republic existed from 1798 to 1803.

39664.q: Which country is the best-known example of a semi-presidential system of government?
39664.e: In France there is a strong president elected by the people and also a prime minister. This mixed form is called a semi-presidential system.
39664.m: France is the classic example of a semi-presidential system.

39665.q: What is typical of a semi-presidential system of government?
a: A president elected by the people and a prime minister who is answerable to parliament
A king and a chancellor, both elected by parliament
A president without a government or parliament
A government of seven members with equal rights
39665.e: Government power is shared between two people. The president is independent of parliament, while the prime minister needs its confidence.
39665.m: In a semi-presidential system, the president and the prime minister share power.

39666.q: Who shaped the constitution of the French Fifth Republic of 1958?
39666.e: Charles de Gaulle wanted a strong president. In 1959 he became the first president of the Fifth Republic.
39666.m: Charles de Gaulle is seen as the father of the Fifth Republic.

39667.q: For how many years is the French president elected today?
39667.e: Since 2002 the term of office has been five years. It used to be seven years.
39667.m: The French president is elected for five years.

39668.q: Who appoints the prime minister in France?
39668.e: The president appoints the prime minister. But the prime minister needs a majority in the National Assembly, otherwise they can be brought down.
39668.m: In France the president appoints the prime minister.

39669.q: What happens if nobody gets an absolute majority in the first round of the French presidential election?
a: There is a run-off between the two leading candidates.
The current president stays in office.
39669.e: The president is elected directly by the people. In the second round, only the two candidates with the most votes take part.
39669.m: If nobody gets an absolute majority, France holds a run-off.

39670.q: What can happen in France if the majority in parliament does not match the president?
a: The president and the prime minister come from opposing camps
The president has to resign immediately
39670.e: The prime minister needs a majority in parliament. If the other side has the majority, opponents govern together. This is called cohabitation.
39670.m: In a cohabitation, political opponents govern France together.

39671.q: What right does the French president have over the National Assembly?
a: He can dissolve it and call new elections.
He can ban its laws for ever.
He can appoint its members himself.
39671.e: The president may dissolve the National Assembly at most once a year. Emmanuel Macron did this in June 2024, for example.
39671.m: The French president can dissolve the National Assembly.

39672.q: Who became Germany's first female Federal Chancellor in 2005?
39672.e: Angela Merkel was Federal Chancellor from 2005 to 2021. She was the first woman in this office.
39672.m: Angela Merkel was the first woman to be German Federal Chancellor.

39673.q: Who is German Federal Chancellor (as of 2025)?
39673.e: Friedrich Merz was elected by the Bundestag on 6 May 2025. He leads a government of the CDU, CSU and SPD.
39673.m: Since May 2025 Friedrich Merz has been German Federal Chancellor.

39674.q: What is the most important task of the German Federal Chancellor?
39674.e: The Federal Chancellor is the head of the German government and sets the direction of policy. The head of state, on the other hand, is the Federal President.
39674.m: The German Federal Chancellor leads the government.

39675.q: Who is head of state of the Federal Republic of Germany?
39675.e: The Federal President represents Germany abroad and signs the laws. But the government is led by the Federal Chancellor.
39675.m: In Germany the Federal President is head of state.

39676.q: What is the official seat of the German head of government in Berlin called?
39676.e: The Federal Chancellery stands in Berlin's government quarter on the River Spree. Bellevue Palace, on the other hand, is the seat of the Federal President.
39676.m: The Federal Chancellor works in the Federal Chancellery in Berlin.

39677.q: Under which Federal Chancellor was Germany reunified in 1990?
39677.e: Helmut Kohl was Federal Chancellor from 1982 to 1998. On 3 October 1990 the GDR joined the Federal Republic.
39677.m: Helmut Kohl was the chancellor of German reunification.

39678.q: Which German Federal Chancellor received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971?
39678.e: Willy Brandt was honoured for his Ostpolitik. He sought reconciliation with Poland, the Soviet Union and the GDR.
39678.m: Willy Brandt received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971.

39679.q: In which building does the German Bundestag meet?
a: In the Reichstag building in Berlin
In the Federal Palace in Bern
In St Paul's Church in Frankfurt
39679.e: Since 1999 the Bundestag has met in the rebuilt Reichstag building in Berlin. Before that its seat was in Bonn.
39679.m: The Bundestag meets in the Reichstag building in Berlin.

39680.q: What are the members of the German Bundestag called?
39680.e: The members of the Bundestag are called members of parliament. They are elected by the people and represent them in parliament.
39680.m: The Bundestag is made up of elected members of parliament.

39681.q: For how many years is the German Bundestag elected?
39681.e: The Bundestag's electoral term lasts four years. If it is dissolved, an election can be held earlier.
39681.m: The Bundestag is elected every four years.

39682.q: What percentage of the second votes does a party normally need to get into the Bundestag?
39682.e: The five per cent hurdle is meant to stop too many small parties sitting in parliament. Exceptions apply, for example, to parties of national minorities.
39682.m: There is a five per cent hurdle for the Bundestag.

39683.q: With which vote do you vote for a party in the Bundestag election?
39683.e: With the first vote you vote for a person in your constituency. The second vote goes to a party and decides how the seats are distributed.
39683.m: The second vote decides the distribution of seats in the Bundestag.

39684.q: What is the main task of the German Bundestag?
a: Representing the country as head of state
39684.e: The Bundestag represents the people and passes the federal laws. It also scrutinises the government and approves the budget.
39684.m: The Bundestag passes the laws in Germany.

39685.q: What is on the roof of the Bundestag building in Berlin and open to visitors?
a: A roof garden with a zoo
39685.e: The glass dome, which you can walk through, was designed by the architect Norman Foster and opened in 1999. From there you can look down into the plenary chamber.
39685.m: There is a glass dome you can walk through on top of the Bundestag building.

39686.q: In Germany, which body represents the federal states in federal law-making?
39686.e: The Bundesrat is made up of representatives of the governments of the 16 federal states. In Switzerland, the Council of States plays a similar role for the cantons.
39686.m: In Germany the Bundesrat represents the federal states.

39688.q: Who normally becomes Prime Minister in the United Kingdom?
a: The leader of the party with the majority in the House of Commons
The oldest member of the House of Lords
The winner of a separate popular vote
39688.e: The Prime Minister needs the support of the House of Commons. That is why the leader of the strongest party is usually appointed.
39688.m: The Prime Minister is usually whoever leads the strongest party in the House of Commons.

39689.q: Who formally appoints the British Prime Minister?
39689.e: Formally, the King or Queen appoints the Prime Minister. In doing so, the monarch follows the majorities in parliament.
39689.m: The British monarch formally appoints the Prime Minister.

39690.q: Who was the first woman to be British Prime Minister?
39690.e: Margaret Thatcher became Prime Minister in 1979 and governed until 1990. Because of her tough policies she was called the “Iron Lady”.
39690.m: From 1979 Margaret Thatcher was the first female British Prime Minister.

39691.q: Where does the British Prime Minister sit as a member of parliament?
39691.e: It has long been the custom for the Prime Minister to be a member of the House of Commons. That way they have to answer directly to the elected members.
39691.m: The British Prime Minister is usually a member of the House of Commons.

39692.q: Where is the British Prime Minister's official residence?
39692.e: The British Prime Minister's official residence is 10 Downing Street in London. Robert Walpole, who is seen as the first Prime Minister, moved in there in 1735.
39692.m: The British Prime Minister works at 10 Downing Street.

39693.q: What role does a prime minister have in a parliamentary system?
39693.e: The prime minister leads the government and the cabinet. The head of state is usually a different person, such as a monarch or a president.
39693.m: A prime minister is the head of the government.

39694.q: What is the weekly question session called in which the British Prime Minister answers questions from members of parliament?
39694.e: Every Wednesday the Prime Minister answers questions in the House of Commons. The verbal battles with the opposition are especially famous.
39694.m: At Prime Minister's Questions, the British head of government has to face questions from members of parliament.

a: A government formed jointly by several parties
A government made up of only one party
A government of experts without a party
39695.e: Several parties join together and share out the ministerial posts. Together they have a majority in parliament.
39695.m: A coalition government is formed by several parties together.

39696.q: Why do parties in many countries form coalitions?
a: Because no party has a majority in parliament on its own
Because the constitution only allows two parties
39696.e: To get laws passed and to form the government, you need a majority. With proportional representation, a single party rarely reaches one.
39696.m: Coalitions are formed when no party has a majority on its own.

39697.q: What is the document called in which parties set out their joint plans for their time in government?
39697.e: The coalition agreement says which goals the partners want to achieve together. It also sets out who gets which ministries.
39697.m: In the coalition agreement, parties set out their joint government goals.

39701.q: What is a government called that has no majority of its own in parliament?
39701.e: A minority government has to look for votes from other parties for every law. Such governments are common in Denmark and Sweden, for example.
39701.m: A minority government has no majority of its own in parliament.

39702.q: What is the minimum number of parties needed for a coalition?
39702.e: A coalition is an alliance. For that you need at least two parties that govern together.
39702.m: A coalition is made up of at least two parties.

39703.q: What is a vote of no confidence?
a: A vote in which parliament withdraws its confidence in the government
A vote by the people on a new law
An election of the head of state by the people
A court ruling against a minister
39703.e: With a vote of no confidence, a parliament can bring down a government. It is an important way of keeping the government in check.
39703.m: With a vote of no confidence, parliament can vote a government out.

39704.q: What often happens in Britain when the government loses a vote of no confidence?
a: The King carries on ruling alone
The government simply stays in office
39704.e: If the government loses the confidence of the House of Commons, it usually has to step down, and there is often a new election. In 1979 a government lost in this way by just one vote.
39704.m: A lost vote of no confidence often leads to a new election.

39705.q: In a constructive vote of no confidence, what must the German Bundestag do at the same time?
39705.e: In Germany, the Bundestag can only vote the chancellor out if it elects a successor at the same time. That way the country is never without a head of government.
39705.m: In a constructive vote of no confidence, a new chancellor is elected straight away.

39706.q: Can the Federal Assembly in Switzerland remove the Federal Council during its term of office with a vote of no confidence?
a: No, the Federal Council is elected for a fixed four years.
Yes, but only at the end of the year
39706.e: In Switzerland there is no vote of no confidence against the Federal Council. Its members stay in office until the next general election of the whole council.
39706.m: Parliament cannot bring down the Swiss Federal Council with a vote of no confidence.

39707.q: What is it called when the head of government asks parliament whether it still supports them?
39707.e: In a confidence vote, the initiative comes from the government. If it loses the vote, this can lead to new elections.
39707.m: With a confidence vote, the head of government checks whether parliament still backs them.

39708.q: What followed after Federal Chancellor Olaf Scholz lost a confidence vote in December 2024?
a: An early Bundestag election in February 2025
39708.e: After the lost vote, the Federal President dissolved the Bundestag. The new election took place on 23 February 2025.
39708.m: Olaf Scholz's lost confidence vote led to an early election in 2025.

39709.q: Which parliament in France can bring down the government with a vote of no confidence?
39709.e: The French National Assembly can withdraw its confidence in the government. In December 2024 it brought down the prime minister in this way.
39709.m: In France the National Assembly can bring down the government.

39710.q: In which system of government does the government depend on the confidence of parliament?
39710.e: In the parliamentary system, the government is supported by parliament and can be brought down by it. That is why the vote of no confidence exists there.
39710.m: In the parliamentary system, the government needs the confidence of parliament.

39711.q: Which two big parties dominate politics in the USA?
39711.e: Since the middle of the 19th century, Democrats or Republicans have provided almost all presidents and members of Congress. This is called a two-party system.
39711.m: Democrats and Republicans dominate in the USA.

39712.q: Which animal is the symbol of the Republican Party in the USA?
39712.e: The elephant became well known in the 19th century through cartoons by Thomas Nast. The Democrats, on the other hand, have the donkey as their symbol.
39712.m: The symbol of the Republicans is the elephant.

39713.q: Which colour stands for the Democratic Party in the USA?
39713.e: On election maps, states with a Democratic majority are coloured blue. The Republicans have the colour red.
39713.m: The Democrats in the USA have the colour blue.

39714.q: Which two parties have provided Britain's prime ministers for about 100 years?
a: Labour and the Scottish National Party
39714.e: Since the 1920s the Conservative Party and the Labour Party have taken turns in government. That is why Britain is seen as an example of a two-party system.
39714.m: In Britain, the Conservatives and Labour take turns in government.

39715.q: Why do small parties in the USA have hardly any chance of winning seats in Congress?
a: Because in each constituency only the candidate with the most votes wins
Because only rich people may vote
Because the President chooses the members
39715.e: In majority voting, only one person wins in each constituency. That is why many people vote straight away for one of the two big parties.
39715.m: Majority voting in constituencies favours big parties.

39716.q: What kind of party system does Switzerland have?
39716.e: Many parties are represented in the National Council, for example the SVP, SP, FDP, Centre, Greens and Green Liberals. No party reaches a majority on its own.

39717.q: How do the big US parties choose their candidates for the presidential election?
a: By appointment by the current President
By a vote in the Senate
39717.e: In primaries and party meetings called caucuses, voters choose between the contenders. The candidate is then officially nominated at the party convention.
39717.m: US parties choose their presidential candidates in primaries.

39718.q: What are the smaller parties in the USA, besides the two big ones, called?
39718.e: Third parties such as the Libertarian Party or the Green Party do stand in elections. But because of the voting system, they hardly win any seats in Congress.
39718.m: Smaller parties in the USA are called third parties.

39719.q: Who sat in judgement at the courts in ancient Athens?
39719.e: In Athens, several hundred citizens chosen by lot often sat in judgement on a case as jurors.
39719.m: In Athens, citizens chosen by lot judged cases as jurors.

39721.q: How did citizens usually vote in the assembly of Athens?
39721.e: The citizens raised their hands and the majority was estimated. Thousands of men gathered in the open air to do this.
39721.m: In the assembly of Athens, people voted by raising their hands.

39722.q: Who was allowed to vote in the assembly of Athens?
a: All the inhabitants of the city
39722.e: Women, slaves and foreigners who had moved there were excluded. So only a small part of the population could have a say.
39722.m: In Athens only adult male citizens could vote.

39723.q: What was ostracism in ancient Athens?
a: A vote that could send a politician into exile
A festival in honour of the gods
39723.e: The citizens scratched the name of a politician who had become too powerful onto pieces of pottery. Whoever got the most votes had to leave Athens for ten years.
39723.m: With ostracism, the Athenians could send a politician into exile.

39724.q: In which city did one of the first democracies arise about 2,500 years ago?
39724.e: Around 508 BC Athens introduced a system in which the citizens themselves had a say. It is seen as the beginning of democracy.

39725.q: How were many offices and seats on the council given out in Athens?
39725.e: Drawing lots was meant to give all citizens the same chance of an office. Only a few offices, such as the generals, were elected.
39725.m: In Athens many offices were given out by lot.

39726.q: What was the task of the council in democratic Athens?
a: It prepared the decisions of the assembly
It led the army in war
39726.e: The council was made up of citizens chosen by lot. It prepared the topics that the assembly then decided on.
39726.m: The council in Athens prepared the assembly's business.

39727.q: What was the agora in ancient Athens?
a: The market place and meeting place of the citizens
The temple of the goddess Athena
39727.e: On the agora people traded, discussed and did politics. It was the centre of public life.
39727.m: The agora was the market place of Athens.

39728.q: Which office did Pericles hold for many years in a row?
39728.e: The strategoi were generals and were elected every year. From 443 BC Pericles was elected several times in a row.
39728.m: Pericles was an elected general of Athens for many years.

39729.q: Which famous temple on the Acropolis was built under Pericles?
39729.e: Work on the Parthenon began in 447 BC. It was dedicated to the goddess Athena.
39729.m: The Parthenon on the Acropolis was built under Pericles.

39730.q: To which goddess was the Parthenon in Athens dedicated?
39730.e: The Parthenon on the Acropolis was built under Pericles for Athena, the patron goddess of Athens. A large statue of the goddess stood in the temple.
39730.m: The Parthenon was dedicated to the goddess Athena.

39731.q: Which innovation does Aristotle credit to Pericles so that poor citizens could also take part?
39731.e: Anyone who served as a juror at court received payment. This meant citizens without wealth could also afford to take part.
39731.m: Daily pay allowed poor Athenians to serve in the courts too.

39732.q: What did Pericles praise in his famous speech for the fallen soldiers?
39732.e: In his Funeral Oration, Pericles praises Athens's form of state, in which many citizens have a say. The speech was recorded by the historian Thucydides.
39732.m: In his Funeral Oration, Pericles praised Athenian democracy.

39733.q: What did Pericles' citizenship law of 451 BC require?
a: You must own land in Athens
You must be able to read and write
You must have served in the army
39733.e: Only those whose father and mother were both Athenian received citizenship. This kept the circle of citizens small.
39733.m: Under Pericles' law, both parents had to be Athenian.

39734.q: Against which city did Athens go to war under Pericles from 431 BC?
39734.e: The Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta lasted until 404 BC and ended with Athens's defeat.
39734.m: From 431 BC Athens fought Sparta in the Peloponnesian War.

39735.q: What punishment did the loser of an ostracism face?
39735.e: Whoever got the most votes had to leave Athens for ten years. After that, he was allowed to return.
39735.m: Ostracism sent a politician into exile for ten years.

39737.q: What happened to the property of someone exiled by ostracism?
a: He was allowed to keep it
39737.e: Ostracism was not a punishment for a crime. The exiled person kept his property and his civic honour.
39737.m: In ostracism, the exiled person kept his property.

39738.q: What was the aim of ostracism in Athens?
a: To prevent rule by one person
39738.e: Politicians who were too powerful could set up a tyranny. The citizens wanted to prevent this with exile.
39738.m: Ostracism was meant to prevent a tyranny.

39739.q: In which city did ostracism exist in ancient times?
39739.e: Ostracism was part of democracy in ancient Athens. With it, citizens could exile politicians who had become too powerful for ten years.

39740.q: How often at most could the assembly hold an ostracism?
39740.e: Every year the assembly decided without debate whether an ostracism should take place. In fact only a few politicians were exiled.
39740.m: An ostracism was possible at most once a year.

39741.q: Who ruled Rome before the Roman Republic came about?
39741.e: According to tradition, the Romans drove out their last king, Tarquinius Superbus, in 509 BC. After that Rome became a republic.
39741.m: Before the republic, Rome was ruled by kings.

39742.q: Where does the word “senate” come from?
a: From the Latin word for “old man”
39742.e: “Senex” means old man in Latin. The senate was originally a council of elders.
39742.m: The senate was originally a council of elders.

39743.q: How many consuls were at the head of the Roman Republic at the same time?
39743.e: Two consuls were elected every year and could keep a check on each other. This was meant to stop anyone getting too much power.
39743.m: The Roman Republic had two consuls every year.

39744.q: How long did a member of the Roman Senate normally stay in office?
39744.e: The Senate was made up mainly of former office holders. They usually kept their seat until death.
39744.m: Roman senators usually sat in the Senate for life.

39745.q: Which office in Rome protected the ordinary citizens, the plebeians?
39745.e: Tribunes of the people could use their veto to stop decisions that harmed the plebeians.
39745.m: The tribune of the people protected the plebeians with his right of veto.

39746.q: When was a dictator given power in the Roman Republic?
a: In an emergency for a short time
After every election for ten years
39746.e: In an emergency, such as a war, a dictator was given a lot of power, but only for six months at most. Caesar later broke this rule.
39746.m: A Roman dictator only ruled in emergencies and for a short time.

39747.q: In which year was Julius Caesar murdered during a meeting of the Senate?
39747.e: On the Ides of March 44 BC senators stabbed Caesar because they saw him as a threat to the republic.
39747.m: Caesar was murdered by senators in 44 BC.

39748.q: Which English king had to seal the Magna Carta in 1215?
39748.e: King John had demanded high taxes and lost wars. After that he had to recognise the rights of his subjects.
39748.m: King John sealed the Magna Carta in 1215.

39749.q: What does the Latin name “Magna Carta” mean?
39749.e: “Magna” means great, and “carta” means charter or document.

39750.q: In which country was the Magna Carta created in 1215?
39750.e: The Magna Carta was sealed in 1215 by the Thames west of London. It is seen as an important document in English history.
39750.m: The Magna Carta comes from England.

39751.q: Which group forced the English king to agree to the Magna Carta in 1215?
39751.e: The powerful nobles, the barons, rebelled against King John. They wanted to limit his power.
39751.m: The barons forced the king to agree to the Magna Carta.

39752.q: In which language was the Magna Carta written?
39752.e: In the Middle Ages, important documents in Europe were usually written in Latin.
39752.m: The Magna Carta was written in Latin.

39753.q: Which principle does the Magna Carta contain?
a: No free man may be imprisoned without a judgement
The king is elected by the people
The church is separate from the state
39753.e: Free men could only be punished after a lawful judgement or according to the law. This idea still shapes the rule of law today.
39753.m: The Magna Carta protected free men from arbitrary imprisonment.

39754.q: Who declared the Magna Carta invalid shortly after 1215?
39754.e: The Pope took King John's side and declared the charter void in August 1215. Later, however, it was issued again.
39754.m: The Pope declared the first Magna Carta invalid.

39755.q: Where can you see an original copy of the 1215 Magna Carta today?
a: In the British Library in London
In the Federal Palace in Bern
39755.e: Two of the four surviving copies are in the British Library in London. The others are in the cathedrals of Lincoln and Salisbury.
39755.m: Copies of the Magna Carta are kept in England today.

39756.q: In which country was the Bill of Rights of 1689 passed?
39756.e: The English Parliament passed the Bill of Rights in 1689 and so strengthened its rights against the king.
39756.m: The Bill of Rights of 1689 comes from England.

39757.q: Which event came directly before the Bill of Rights of 1689?
39757.e: In 1688 the king was overthrown without much bloodshed. This is called the Glorious Revolution.
39757.m: The Bill of Rights followed the Glorious Revolution.

39758.q: What is the Bill of Rights of 1689?
a: A law that strengthened the rights of parliament
39758.e: In it, the English Parliament set out what the king was no longer allowed to do without its consent.
39758.m: The Bill of Rights strengthened parliament against the king.

39759.q: Who gained more power through the Bill of Rights?
39759.e: For example, the king could no longer raise taxes without the consent of parliament. This made parliament stronger.
39759.m: The Bill of Rights gave parliament more power.

39760.q: Under the Bill of Rights, what could the king only do with the consent of parliament?
39760.e: Without parliament, the king could not collect money from the people. This gave parliament a strong means of pressure.
39760.m: After the Bill of Rights, the king needed parliament for taxes.

39761.q: Which right did the Bill of Rights guarantee members of parliament?
39761.e: What was said in parliament could not be prosecuted in any court. This meant members could debate freely.
39761.m: The Bill of Rights gave members of parliament freedom of speech.

39762.q: According to the Bill of Rights, what was the king not allowed to keep in peacetime without parliament?
39762.e: An army in peacetime needed the consent of parliament. The king was not to be able to use an army against his own people.
39762.m: Without parliament, the king could not keep a standing army in peacetime.

39763.q: Which form of state developed in England after the Bill of Rights?
39763.e: The king remained head of state, but parliament gained more and more power. This system still exists in the United Kingdom today.
39763.m: After the Bill of Rights, a parliamentary monarchy developed in England.

39764.q: Who was the main author of the US Declaration of Independence?
39764.e: Jefferson wrote the draft, which a committee including Benjamin Franklin and John Adams revised. He later became the third President of the USA.
39764.m: Thomas Jefferson wrote the US Declaration of Independence.

39765.q: In which city was the US Declaration of Independence adopted?
39765.e: The Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in what is now Independence Hall.
39765.m: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in Philadelphia.

39766.q: From which country did the American colonies declare independence in 1776?
39766.e: The colonies resisted taxes and laws of the British King George III.
39766.m: The USA broke away from Britain in 1776.

39767.q: How many colonies declared their independence together in 1776?
39767.e: The 13 stripes on the US flag are still a reminder of these founding colonies today.
39767.m: Thirteen colonies declared their independence in 1776.

39768.q: Which rights does the US Declaration of Independence name as unalienable?
a: Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
39768.e: According to the Declaration, all men are created equal and have these rights from birth.
39768.m: The Declaration of Independence names life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

39769.q: Which assembly adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776?
39769.e: The Continental Congress was made up of representatives of all the colonies. The Senate only came into being with the constitution of 1787.
39769.m: The Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence.

39770.q: On which day does the USA celebrate its independence?
39770.e: On 4 July 1776 the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. That is why 4 July is the national holiday of the USA.
39770.m: The USA celebrates its independence on 4 July.

39771.q: Who signed the US Declaration of Independence?
39771.e: 56 representatives from all 13 colonies signed the Declaration. The British king was the opponent they wanted to break away from.
39771.m: Representatives of all 13 colonies signed the Declaration of Independence.

39772.q: In which year was the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen proclaimed in France?
39772.e: It was written in the first year of the French Revolution, on 26 August 1789.
39772.m: France proclaimed the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in 1789.

39773.q: Which assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in 1789?
39773.e: The representatives of the Third Estate had declared themselves the National Assembly and wanted to give France a constitution.
39773.m: The French National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man.

39775.q: What does the first article of the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen say?
a: People are born free and equal in rights
39775.e: The first article says that all people are born free and equal in rights. This was a big break with the privileges of the nobility and the king.
39775.m: According to the 1789 Declaration, all people are free and equal in rights.

39776.q: Which event on 14 July 1789 came before the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen?
39776.e: People in Paris stormed the Bastille prison, a symbol of royal power. Today 14 July is France's national holiday.
39776.m: The storming of the Bastille was on 14 July 1789.

39777.q: Which woman wrote a “Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen” in 1791?
39777.e: Olympe de Gouges criticised the fact that the 1789 Declaration forgot women. She demanded equal rights for women.
39777.m: In 1791 Olympe de Gouges demanded equal rights for women.

39778.q: What is the famous motto of the French Revolution?
a: Un pour tous, tous pour un
39778.e: The words mean liberty, equality, fraternity. Today they are France's official motto.
39778.m: Liberty, equality, fraternity is the motto of France.

39779.q: Which principle does the 1789 Declaration require for every constitution?
39779.e: According to the Declaration, a society without guaranteed rights and without separation of powers has no constitution. So power should be divided among several bodies.
39779.m: The 1789 Declaration requires the separation of powers.

39780.q: What does the English word “suffrage”, from which “suffragette” comes, mean?
39780.e: “Suffrage” means the right to vote. The suffragettes fought for women's right to vote.
39780.m: The word “suffrage” means the right to vote.

39781.q: Who founded the suffragettes' women's organisation in Manchester in 1903?
39781.e: Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union together with her daughters.
39781.m: Emmeline Pankhurst founded the suffragettes' organisation.

39782.q: What was the motto of Emmeline Pankhurst's suffragette organisation?
39782.e: The suffragettes wanted to attract attention with actions instead of just asking.
39782.m: The motto of the suffragettes was “Deeds, not words”.

39783.q: How did many suffragettes protest when they were in prison?
39783.e: Many suffragettes refused to eat in prison. The authorities then often fed them by force.
39783.m: Many suffragettes went on hunger strike in prison.

39784.q: How did the suffragettes draw attention to their demand for women's right to vote?
a: With secret letters to their friends
39784.e: The suffragettes demonstrated, disrupted events and even smashed windows. In 1913 Emily Wilding Davison ran onto the track at the horse race in Epsom and died of her injuries.
39784.m: The suffragettes fought for women's right to vote with eye-catching actions.

39785.q: Which colours did the suffragettes wear as a sign of recognition?
39785.e: Purple stood for dignity, white for purity and green for hope.
39785.m: The suffragettes wore purple, white and green.

39786.q: In which year did women in Britain get the same right to vote as men?
39786.e: In 1918, at first only women aged 30 and over who met certain conditions could vote. From 1928 the same voting age of 21 applied to women and men.
39786.m: Since 1928 women in Britain have voted on equal terms with men.

39787.q: What were the women's rights campaigners in Britain called who fought for the vote only by peaceful means?
39787.e: The suffragists around Millicent Fawcett relied on petitions and talks instead of attention-grabbing actions.
39787.m: The moderate women's rights campaigners were called suffragists.

39788.q: Which country was the first self-governing country to introduce women's right to vote at national level, in 1893?
39788.e: At that time New Zealand was a British colony with its own government. Women voted for the first time on 28 November 1893.
39788.m: In 1893 New Zealand was the first country to introduce women's right to vote.

39789.q: What were women in New Zealand allowed to do from 1893?
a: Go to school for the first time
Drive a car for the first time
Become a Federal Councillor for the first time
39789.e: Since 1893 women in New Zealand have been able to vote in elections for parliament. This made New Zealand a model for the world.
39789.m: Women in New Zealand have voted since 1893.

39790.q: How did many people in New Zealand show in 1893 that they wanted women's right to vote?
a: With a petition full of signatures
With a popular initiative like in Switzerland
39790.e: Thousands signed a large petition to parliament. The sheets glued together were many metres long.
39790.m: A large petition helped the women in New Zealand.

a: A campaigner for women's right to vote in New Zealand
39791.e: Kate Sheppard collected signatures and won over politicians. Today she even appears on a New Zealand banknote.
39791.m: Kate Sheppard campaigned for women's right to vote in New Zealand.

39792.q: To which country did New Zealand belong as a colony in 1893?
39792.e: New Zealand was a British colony with its own government. That is why it could pass its own electoral law.
39792.m: In 1893 New Zealand was a British colony.

39793.q: What were women in New Zealand not yet allowed to do in 1893?
39793.e: In 1893 women only got the right to vote. They were only allowed to stand as candidates themselves a few years later.
39793.m: Being allowed to vote and being elected are two different rights.

39794.q: Were Māori women also allowed to vote in New Zealand in 1893?
a: Yes, they also got the right to vote
39794.e: The 1893 law applied to women of European origin and to Māori women. The Māori voted in their own constituencies.
39794.m: In New Zealand, Māori women could also vote in 1893.

39795.q: How many years after New Zealand (1893) did Switzerland introduce women's suffrage at federal level in 1971?
39795.e: Calculation: 1971 minus 1893 = 78. Switzerland was one of the last countries in Europe.
39795.m: Switzerland introduced women's suffrage 78 years after New Zealand.

39796.q: In which city does the Australian parliament meet?
39796.e: Canberra is the capital of Australia. The Parliament House is there, even though Sydney and Melbourne are bigger.
39796.m: The Australian parliament meets in the capital, Canberra.

a: You have to go and vote
You are not allowed to vote
You may only vote once in your life
You have to stand as a candidate
39797.e: With compulsory voting, everyone entitled to vote has to vote. In Australia, anyone who does not vote without a reason pays a fine.
39797.m: Compulsory voting means you have to go and vote.

39798.q: What happens in Australia if you do not vote without a good reason?
39798.e: Anyone who does not vote has to pay a fine if they cannot give a valid reason.
39798.m: Anyone in Australia who does not vote without a reason pays a fine.

39799.q: Because of compulsory voting, how high is turnout in Australia usually?
39799.e: Usually over 90 per cent of those registered cast their vote. In comparison, turnout in Switzerland is often below 50 per cent.
39799.m: Thanks to compulsory voting, usually over 90 per cent vote in Australia.

39800.q: On which day of the week are national elections in Australia always held?
39800.e: Saturday is a day off work for many people. That makes voting easier.
39800.m: In Australia people always vote on a Saturday.

39801.q: From what age do you have to register on the electoral roll in Australia?
39801.e: Registering is compulsory from 18. At 16 or 17 you can register in advance voluntarily, but you can only vote from 18.
39801.m: In Australia you have to register as a voter from the age of 18.

39802.q: What do voters do on the ballot paper in the election for the Australian House of Representatives?
a: They put a ball into an urn
39802.e: You rank all the candidates in order of preference with numbers. That way your further choices also count if your favourite is knocked out.
39802.m: In Australia you number the candidates in order of preference.

39803.q: What do volunteers in Australia often sell outside polling stations on election day?
39803.e: The so-called “democracy sausage” is a sausage in bread. Schools and clubs use the money raised to support their projects.
39803.m: In Australia, a barbecued sausage outside the polling station is part of election day.

39804.q: Why do people in Australia, as in Switzerland, fill in their ballot paper in secret?
a: So that nobody sees who they vote for
So that the vote is quicker
So that they do not lose the paper
39804.e: The secret ballot with official ballot papers was introduced in Australia in 1856. It protects each person's free decision.
39804.m: The secret ballot protects people's free decision.

39805.q: Why did India's first parliamentary election in 1951/52 take several months?
a: The country was huge and a great many people voted
The votes were recounted every day
The election was banned every week
Only one person could vote per day
39805.e: India is very large and even then had hundreds of millions of inhabitants. That is why voting took place in many stages from October 1951 to February 1952.
39805.m: Because of the size of the country, India's first election took months.

39806.q: From which country did India become independent in 1947, before electing its first parliament in 1951/52?
39806.e: India was a British colony for a long time and became independent in 1947. A few years later the people elected their parliament for the first time.
39806.m: India became independent from Britain in 1947.

39808.q: What was special about India's first parliamentary election in 1951/52?
a: It was the largest election in the world at the time
There was only a single candidate
39808.e: About 173 million people were entitled to vote. No democratic election had ever been so large before.
39808.m: India's first election was the largest democratic election in the world at the time.

39809.q: Who was allowed to vote in India's first parliamentary election?
39809.e: From the start, India gave all adults the same right to vote, whether woman or man, rich or poor. At that time it applied from the age of 21.
39809.m: All adults could vote in India's first election.

39810.q: How were people who could not read helped in India's first election?
a: With readers in the voting booth
With voting by show of hands
39810.e: Each candidate had their own ballot box with their name and a symbol. That way people could vote correctly even without being able to read.
39810.m: Symbols helped people who could not read in India's first election.

39811.q: What was the task of the Election Commission in India's first election?
39811.e: The Election Commission under Sukumar Sen planned the election with hundreds of thousands of polling stations. It made sure that everyone entitled to vote could do so.
39811.m: An election commission organises the elections.

39812.q: How many chambers does the Indian parliament have?
39812.e: The Indian parliament has two chambers. The Lok Sabha, the “House of the People”, is elected by the people. The Rajya Sabha represents the states.
39812.m: Like the Swiss parliament, the Indian parliament has two chambers.

39813.q: What form of state has India had since its constitution of 1950?
39813.e: With the constitution of 26 January 1950, India became a republic. Since then the people have elected their parliament, and there is no king.
39813.m: India has been a republic since 1950.

39814.q: What does the third Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which Switzerland has also ratified, allow?
a: Children can complain to the UN
Children no longer have to go to school
39814.e: With the third Optional Protocol, children whose rights have been violated can send a communication to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. Before that, however, they have to use up all legal options in their own country.
39814.m: Thanks to an optional protocol, children can complain to the UN.

39815.q: According to Article 12, what should a child's opinion be taken into account according to?
39815.e: The child's opinion is taken into account appropriately and in line with their age and maturity. The older and more mature a child is, the more weight their opinion has.
39815.m: The more mature a child is, the more their opinion counts.

39816.q: What does the right to have a say under Article 12 NOT mean?
a: The child may give their opinion
39816.e: Having a say means that the child is heard and their opinion goes into the decision. But responsibility for the decision often lies with adults or authorities.
39816.m: Having a say means being heard, but not always deciding alone.

39817.q: According to Article 12, where does a child expressly have the right to be heard?
39817.e: Paragraph 2 of Article 12 requires that a child be heard in court and administrative proceedings that affect them, either directly or through a representative.
39817.m: Children may also give their view in court and before authorities.

39818.q: Under Article 12, does a child always have to give their opinion?
a: No, they may, but they do not have to
Yes, they are legally obliged to
Only if their parents demand it
39818.e: Article 12 gives the child a right, not a duty. So a child can also decide that they do not want to comment on a question.
39818.m: Having a say is a right, not a duty.

39819.q: Who can represent a child's interests in court proceedings in Switzerland?
39819.e: A court can appoint a representative for the child, often a lawyer or a specialist. They bring the child's point of view into the proceedings.
39819.m: A child's representative brings the child's view to court.

39820.q: Which word from Latin describes children and young people having a say?
39820.e: Participation comes from the Latin “participare”, to take part. It means that children are involved in decisions that affect them.

39821.q: Which of the four basic principles of the Convention on the Rights of the Child is in Article 12?
39821.e: The Convention has four basic principles: non-discrimination, the best interests of the child, the right to life and development, and participation. Participation is set out in Article 12.
39821.m: Participation is a basic principle of children's rights.

39822.q: Which UN body checks whether states are putting children's rights into practice?
a: The Committee on the Rights of the Child
39822.e: States regularly send reports to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. It examines them and makes recommendations, including to Switzerland.
39822.m: A UN committee checks how children's rights are put into practice.

39824.q: What is a typical aim of a children's parliament?
39824.e: In a children's parliament, children learn to put forward concerns, discuss them and vote. In this way they practise democracy on a small scale.
39824.m: In a children's parliament, children learn how democracy works.

39825.q: What is the body for older young people that is similar to a children's parliament called?
39825.e: Many municipalities and cantons have youth parliaments for young people. They work in a similar way to children's parliaments but often deal with more political topics.
39825.m: Young people can take part in a youth parliament.

39826.q: How are decisions usually made in a children's parliament?
39826.e: As in a real parliament, the children's parliament votes on proposals. Whatever the majority wants is accepted.
39826.m: In a children's parliament, the majority decides.

39827.q: Which concern fits best in a municipality's children's parliament?
39827.e: Children's parliaments deal with topics from the children's everyday life where they live, for example playgrounds, routes to school or leisure activities.
39827.m: Children's parliaments deal with topics from children's everyday lives.

39828.q: What do some children's parliaments in Switzerland get from their municipality so they can carry out their own projects?
39828.e: Some municipalities give their children's parliament a small sum of money. The children then decide themselves which projects to support with it.
39828.m: With their own budget, children can carry out projects themselves.

39829.q: How does a decision of a children's parliament usually reach the adults in politics?
a: As a proposal to the municipal authority
39829.e: The children's parliament can send proposals or wishes to the municipal council or town parliament. These authorities then consider whether to put the idea into practice.
39829.m: Children's parliaments submit their concerns to the municipality.

39830.q: Why is it called a children's parliament?
a: It meets in the Federal Palace
It is elected by the people
39830.e: A parliament is an assembly that discusses and votes. The children's parliament copies this way of working, but it has no power to make laws.
39830.m: A children's parliament works on the model of a parliament.

39831.q: Who usually represents a class on the pupils' council?
39831.e: Each class elects one or two representatives. They bring the class's concerns to the pupils' council and report back afterwards.
39831.m: Class representatives bring their class's wishes to the pupils' council.

39832.q: What is the regular meeting within a single class called, at which concerns are collected?
39832.e: In the class council, pupils discuss problems and ideas in their class. They can then pass important concerns on to the pupils' council.
39832.m: In the class council, a class discusses its concerns.

39833.q: Which topic can a pupils' council typically have a say on?
39833.e: A pupils' council puts forward ideas about school life, such as the playground, project days or rules in the school building. It does not decide on marks or hiring.
39833.m: The pupils' council has a say in everyday school life.

39834.q: What do pupils learn in particular on the pupils' council?
39834.e: On the pupils' council, children and young people practise giving reasons for an opinion, listening and finding compromises. These are important democratic skills.
39834.m: On the pupils' council you practise representing concerns.

39835.q: What records what was discussed and decided on the pupils' council?
39835.e: The minutes record the most important discussions and decisions. That way everyone knows later what was agreed.

39836.q: Who usually supports a pupils' council?
39836.e: Usually a teacher or a school social worker supports the pupils' council. They help with organising it but do not decide in place of the children.
39836.m: An adult supporter helps the pupils' council.

39837.q: Why is a pupils' council an example of representative democracy?
39837.e: In a representative democracy, people elect representatives who decide for them. On the pupils' council, the representatives stand for their whole class.
39837.m: On the pupils' council, elected pupils represent their classmates.

39838.q: What should class representatives do after a meeting of the pupils' council?
39838.e: Representatives are the link between the class and the pupils' council. They tell their class about the decisions and take new concerns with them.
39838.m: Representatives tell their class about the pupils' council.

39839.q: Where does the plenary meeting of the Federal Youth Session take place?
a: In the National Council chamber in Bern
At the UN headquarters in Geneva
At the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
39839.e: The young people discuss in working groups and meet at the end in the National Council chamber of the Federal Palace. There they vote on their demands.
39839.m: The Youth Session meets in the Federal Palace in Bern.

39840.q: What can parliamentary committees do with a petition from the Youth Session?
a: Take up the concern with a parliamentary proposal
Put it straight into force as a law
Hand it to the Federal Supreme Court
39840.e: The committees examine the petition. They can follow up the concern, for example with a motion or a postulate, or propose that no action be taken on it.
39840.m: Committees can take up concerns from the Youth Session.

39841.q: Where are the Youth Session's demands first worked out?
39841.e: The participants work in themed working groups, supported by experts and members of parliament. Only after that do the demands go to the plenary meeting.
39841.m: The demands are worked out in working groups.

39842.q: Who mainly organises the Federal Youth Session?
39842.e: An organising committee of young volunteers aged roughly 16 to 25 plans the event. So the Youth Session is created by young people for young people.
39842.m: Young volunteers organise the Youth Session.

39843.q: What criticism is sometimes made of the Federal Youth Session?
a: That it has little direct influence
That it is too expensive for taxpayers
39843.e: Critics complain that petitions rarely achieve anything directly. Supporters, on the other hand, stress that young people experience politics in practice there.
39843.m: The influence of the Youth Session is debated.

39844.q: In what form are the accepted demands of the Youth Session handed to the federal parliament?
39844.e: The demands go to parliament as petitions. The responsible committees have to deal with them but are not obliged to put them into practice.
39844.m: Demands of the Youth Session are submitted as petitions.

39845.q: Apart from the debates, what else is part of the Youth Session programme?
a: An election campaign for the National Council
39845.e: The supporting programme includes meetings with members of parliament, a games evening and a party. This helps the participants get to know each other.
39845.m: At the Youth Session, young people meet real politicians.

39846.q: How are the topics of the Federal Youth Session chosen?
39846.e: Young people can vote online in advance on which topics will be dealt with. In this way young people help decide the content themselves.
39846.m: The topics of the Youth Session are chosen online.

39847.q: Which group has worked since 2001 to make sure the Youth Session's demands are followed up?
39847.e: About ten young people are involved in the Youth Session Forum. They follow the petitions and keep in contact with members of parliament.
39847.m: The Youth Session Forum follows up the demands.

39848.q: Who started a school strike for the climate in Stockholm in 2018?
39848.e: In August 2018 Greta Thunberg, who was 15 at the time, sat down in front of the Swedish parliament. Her protest inspired young people all over the world, including in Switzerland.
39848.m: Greta Thunberg started the climate strikes in 2018.

39849.q: What does the name of the movement “Fridays for Future” refer to?
39849.e: The young people went on strike on Fridays for more climate protection.
39849.m: Fridays for Future means Fridays for the future.

39850.q: On which day of the week did the school strikes for the climate usually take place?
39850.e: The Fridays for Future movement is named after Friday. On that day pupils stayed away from lessons to demonstrate.
39850.m: The climate strikes usually took place on a Friday.

39851.q: When did the big climate strikes by pupils begin in Switzerland?
39851.e: In December 2018 many young people demonstrated for the climate for the first time in Zurich and other cities. From early 2019 there were regular strikes.
39851.m: The Swiss climate strike movement began at the end of 2018.

39852.q: In which city did the largest climate demonstration in Switzerland, with about 100,000 people, take place in September 2019?
39852.e: On 28 September 2019, according to the organisers, about 100,000 people marched through Bern. It was one of the largest demonstrations in Swiss history.
39852.m: The largest climate demonstration in Switzerland took place in Bern in 2019.

39853.q: By when does Climate Strike Switzerland demand net zero greenhouse gas emissions within the country?
39853.e: The Climate Strike demands net zero by 2030. That is much earlier than the federal government's target of 2050.
39853.m: The Climate Strike demands net zero by 2030.

39854.q: What does the Climate Strike want when it calls for a “climate emergency” to be declared?
a: All cars should be banned immediately
39854.e: With a climate emergency, politicians are meant to recognise that the climate crisis is urgent. Decisions should first be checked for their effects on the climate.
39854.m: A climate emergency is meant to make climate protection a priority.

39855.q: How is the Climate Strike Switzerland movement organised?
a: As a grassroots democracy in local groups
39855.e: The Climate Strike has no party ties and no fixed leadership. Decisions are made in open meetings, and there are regional groups in almost all cantons.
39855.m: The Climate Strike is a grassroots democratic movement.

39856.q: What does easyvote offer young people?
39856.e: Easyvote explains proposals in votes and elections in a way that is easy to understand. It stays politically neutral and gives no voting recommendation.
39856.m: Easyvote explains votes simply and neutrally.

a: The Swiss Federation of Youth Parliaments
39857.e: Easyvote is run by the Swiss Federation of Youth Parliaments, DSJ for short. It encourages young people to take part in politics.
39857.m: Easyvote belongs to the Swiss Federation of Youth Parliaments.

39858.q: What does easyvote NOT give about a vote?
39858.e: Easyvote presents the arguments of both sides but does not say how to vote. The decision stays with the voters.
39858.m: Easyvote does not say how to vote.

39859.q: Why is easyvote mainly meant for young adults?
a: So that more young people go and vote
Because only young people may vote
Because older people do not vote
39859.e: In Switzerland, young adults take part in votes less often than older people. Clear information is meant to make it easier for them to get started.
39859.m: Easyvote wants to get more young people to the ballot box.

39860.q: Which format does easyvote use to explain proposals especially briefly and clearly?
39860.e: Easyvote publishes short explainer clips and infographics about the proposals. They work well on social media and in lessons.
39860.m: Short explainer clips make votes easy to understand.

39861.q: What does the term turnout mean?
a: The share of eligible voters who vote
The number of proposals being voted on
39861.e: Turnout shows what percentage of eligible voters actually voted. Among young people it is often lower than among older people.
39861.m: Turnout shows how many eligible voters take part.

39862.q: In which special form does easyvote also explain votes so that everyone understands them?
39862.e: Easyvote offers texts in Easy Read language. They use short sentences and simple words so that people with reading difficulties can have a say too.
39862.m: Easy Read language makes voting information understandable for everyone.

39863.q: What is easyvote's app called that reminds you about votes?
39863.e: With the votenow app you get information about upcoming votes and elections. That way you never miss a voting date.
39863.m: The votenow app reminds you about votes.

39864.q: Which fundamental right in the Federal Constitution allows people to gather peacefully for a demonstration?
39864.e: The Federal Constitution guarantees freedom of assembly as a fundamental right. Everyone may take part in or organise peaceful gatherings.
39864.m: Freedom of assembly protects peaceful demonstrations.

39866.q: In Switzerland, where do you usually have to apply for a permit for a demonstration on the street?
39866.e: Anyone using public spaces such as streets and squares for a rally usually needs a permit from the municipality or town. The police or a town office is often responsible.
39866.m: A demonstration on public land is usually approved by the municipality.

39867.q: Why does a demonstration on public streets usually need a permit?
a: Because public space is used in a special way
